problem: lightroom clarity setting concert low light white balance photo editing fast turnaround
symptom: Concert / low-light photos look flat or the crowd is too dark, and unsure what white balance to set under shifting stage lighting.
technique: Genre-split clarity + Auto-WB-then-tweak (field tip)
exact_steps: Clarity by genre: for lifestyle/portrait shots DECREASE clarity slightly (softer skin/look); for concert and low-light shots INCREASE clarity a little (not too much) because it brightens the crowd and pulls more crowd detail out of the shadows. White balance: shooting under unpredictable stage lighting, shoot Auto WB in-camera (the camera does a decent job as conditions swing); if a fixed number is needed, ~5600K is the fallback pick (the video team in this clip locked 4350K for matched video). Keep WB consistent through the night, then correct/tweak per-shot in Lightroom afterward rather than chasing it live. For 4am fast turnaround, lean on saved Lightroom presets to batch the base look.
inputs_needed: RAW concert/low-light or lifestyle frames; a saved Lightroom preset for the base look
output_artifact: Edited frames with genre-appropriate clarity and corrected white balance
when_to_use: Fast-turnaround concert/event or low-light edits where lighting shifts constantly and a same-night gallery is due.
when_not: Controlled studio shoots with fixed lighting (set WB to a measured value; clarity choice is per the SNIPED v3 luxury look, which favors restraint over a clarity push). Not a color-grade or LUT workflow.

technique: Lightroom Point Color + Variance slider

problem: reduce noise high ISO, sharpen without sharpening grain, mask sharpening, clarity dehaze

technique: Lightroom Detail panel: noise reduction + masked sharpening
exact_steps: Zoom to 1:1 (click 1:1 in toolbar) to judge noise/sharpness. Hold Alt/Option and drag the Masking slider to see a grayscale mask: black = protected, white = sharpened edges, so you avoid sharpening sky grain. For midtone punch use Clarity (Effects panel); use Dehaze to cut haze (lower Saturation/Vibrance if it over-saturates).

problem: brush local adjustment, auto mask edges, enhance eyes brows lips, silhouette a subject

technique: Lightroom Brush tool with Auto Mask (local portrait retouch / silhouette)
exact_steps: Choose the Brush tool; size with Size slider or [ and ] keys. Open brush settings (triangle by Brush slider). Check Auto Mask (samples color/tone where you start to stay inside edges); set Feather 0 for crisp edges (or high Feather for soft). Raise Flow for faster build, Density to limit transparency. Press O to toggle the red overlay and confirm coverage. Brush the region, then adjust sliders. Portrait sample edits: brows Exposure -0.30 / Blacks -7 / Clarity +11; eyelashes Exposure -0.44 / Blacks -17; whites of eyes Exposure +0.40; irises Temp +4 / Exposure +0.30; lips Tint +5 / Exposure -0.25 / Saturation +20. Click (+) for each new brushed region. For silhouette: brush subject then Exposure -4.00, Highlights -100, Shadows -100, Blacks -100. Uncheck Auto Mask + use Eraser to fix spillover; press / to compare before/after.

problem: build lightroom base preset, master portrait preset, expensive editorial look, warm skin cool background, my edit style

Tone curve: classic S-curve with bottom-left Blacks anchor LIFTED up the Y-axis (e.g. Input 0 / Output 10) for matte editorial wash; pull shadows down slightly, push highlights up slightly, midtones locked center. HSL: Orange Hue +5 (toward gold), Orange Saturation -10, Orange Luminance +15 (glow); Green/Aqua Saturation -30 to -50. Color Grading (split tone): Highlights Hue ~45 warm gold Sat 5-10%, Shadows Hue ~220 deep teal Sat 5-10%, Midtones 0; keep all grading saturation under 15%. Basics: Texture -10, Clarity +5, Vibrance +15, Saturation 0 to -5. Save as preset; tweak only Exposure + White Balance per image (raise Kelvin for golden, lower for moody). Locked numeric variant (Sniped Base V2): tone curve points (0,3)(45,25)(128,135)(190,200)(255,235); color grading shadows Hue225/Sat25/Lum-10, mids Hue25/Sat10, highlights Hue40/Sat18/Lum+5, blending 65 balance -15; HSL green sat -35 yellow -12 aqua -40 blue -30; calibration Red Hue-8 Sat+5, Green Hue+20 Sat-15, Blue Hue+8 Sat+10; sharpening 15 masking 70, NR luminance 10; vignette amount -8 midpoint 25 feather 60 highlights 60.

problem: how to use histogram, set exposure lightroom, avoid blown highlights, whites blacks clipping
symptom: unsure if exposure is right, eyes deceived by screen, blown or crushed detail
technique: Histogram-driven exposure with Alt-drag white/black points
exact_steps: Trust histogram, not screen. Histogram = pixel brightness graph: far left pure black (no detail), center midtones (skin lives here), far right pure white (blown). Set Exposure first: push until skin midtones read correctly without graph slamming the right wall. Contrast slider 10-20 only for portraits (more crushes shadows/blows highlights; use tone curve for heavier contrast). Highlights/Whites negative to recover bright detail; Shadows/Blacks to lift or crush darks. Set true white: hold Alt/Option while dragging Whites right until pixels just appear. Set true black: hold Alt/Option dragging Blacks left until pixels appear. Use clipping warnings to stop just before specular red (highlight) or blue (shadow) clip indicators show.
inputs_needed: RAW file, Lightroom Basic panel + histogram
output_artifact: correctly exposed image with set white/black points
when_to_use: first step of every develop, before tone curve / HSL / grading
when_not: do not use the Auto button then dial back; control the math manually
example_command: os_technique_cards solve "set correct exposure with the histogram and alt-drag white and black points in Lightroom"

problem: matte editorial shadows, faded film look, precision contrast, lifted blacks, tone curve
symptom: basic contrast slider crushes shadows, image looks like cheap snapshot, want expensive matte wash
technique: Lifted-black S-curve plus color curves
exact_steps: Use tone curve, not Contrast slider, for heavy contrast. Classic S-curve: pull shadows down slightly, push highlights up slightly, keep midtones natural. Matte/faded look: lift the bottom-left anchor point of the curve to raise the black point (washed-out film quality in shadows). Specular push for hard-flash look: nudge the top-right node strictly UP the Y-axis to force shiny skin highlights to pop while lifted blacks keep shadows grounded. Color curves: push up the red curve in shadows to add warmth; pull down the blue curve in highlights for yellow warmth.

when_to_use: after exposure set, when you need engineered contrast and the cinematic matte fade

Texture and Clarity -30 to smooth digital noise into a clean seamless sweep. For a focused spotlight/gelled-snoot look instead of full flood: intersect the Background mask with a Radial Gradient drawn behind the head; to convert to full seamless flood, delete the Radial Gradient component so the whole wall floods.

problem: fake bounce light, color spill on subject, light wrap, make composite look real, rim spill
symptom: recolored background looks like a cheap cutout because subject has no matching color bounce
technique: Subject mask intersected with Linear Gradient for fake bounce/spill
exact_steps: Masks > Subject (new mask). Click the three dots > Intersect Mask With > Linear Gradient. Drag the gradient from the outside frame edge INWARD, stopping just as it wraps the side of face/neck/shoulder (bounce light is lazy: keep it on the extreme outer edge only, off the front planes of cheek/nose). Match background color: Color Block Hue = background Hue, Saturation ~50 (light loses saturation as it bounces, drop from the background's 85), Exposure +0.25 to +0.30 (MUST be positive; bounce adds light), Highlights -15 to -20 so spill wraps smoothly without blowing out skin. If spill bleeds onto skin/face, click Subtract and brush it off the face. Fix for over-wrapped mask: grab center pin and drag hard toward the frame edge.

problem: colored spill turns black shirt muddy, protect deep blacks, black wardrobe muddy gray, luminance range mask
symptom: dropping colored bounce over black fabric turns it milky gray-blue/pink because black does not bounce color
technique: Luminance Range intersection to protect black fabric from spill
exact_steps: Build the spill mask: Subject mask intersected with Linear Gradient over the unlit edge. Then click the three dots again > Intersect Mask With > Luminance Range. In the Luminance Range panel grab the LEFT (darks) side of the slider and pull it right, away from the shadows, so the colored bounce applies only to midtones/highlights (skin, hair, shiny specular folds) and NOT the deep black shirt shadows. Watch the mask overlay: ensure color drops off the deep black fabric but stays on skin/hair. Also recover black-fabric volume globally: Basic panel Shadows +15 to +20 (reveals weave/seams), Blacks -5 (keeps it dense). For background color behind black wardrobe use Power Matrices: Aggressive Red (Hue red Sat high), Luxury Emerald/Teal (Hue 150-160 Sat 70 Exposure +0.50), or Void (drop bg exposure, requires real on-set rim light or subject melts).

problem: fake 3D depth, atmospheric perspective, background falloff, more depth from flat wall, lens blur grit
symptom: subject looks pasted onto a flat evenly-lit wall, no Z-axis separation
technique: Three pillars of digital depth (lens blur + shadow anchor + temperature matrix)
exact_steps: 1 Atmospheric depth: before adding background grain, open the Lens Blur module and set Blur Amount low 15-20 to mimic medium-format optical drop-off (sharp subject jumps forward). 2 Luminance depth (shadow anchor): add a Linear Gradient to the Background Mask, drag from the floor UP to the subject's waist, drop Exposure -0.50 to fake light fall-off / inverse-square law and ground the subject. 3 Color depth (temperature matrix): warm advances, cool recedes. Expansive Matrix (deep depth): warm subject/skin + cool background (navy, emerald, toxic cyan) pushes subject forward. Claustrophobic Matrix (aggressive 2D graphic): warm-on-warm (red shirt on crimson, mustard on ochre) flattens depth for poster tension.

problem: how to crop portrait, where to crop limbs, amputated joints, signature crop, geometry panel warp
symptom: crops land on elbows/knees/ankles making subject look dismembered; subject floats in frame
technique: Intentional Slice crop rule + Geometry-panel warning
exact_steps: Never crop directly on elbows, wrists, knees, or ankles (looks amputated). Always slice through mid-bicep, mid-forearm, or mid-thigh; this anchors the subject to the frame edges and turns them into a monumental graphic element instead of a floating person. Delete distracting hands by cropping above them. For 4:5 IG recrop, shift subject off-center leaving negative space on the side the eyes point toward. Geometry/Transform panel: leave OFF for tight studio portraits (Vertical/Horizontal/Distortion warps the skull and stretches proportions); only use it to correct converging architectural lines in environmental shots.

exact_steps: Pipeline split: Lightroom owns global color math, background color shifts, depth, and engineered grit; Evoto owns ONLY the final 5% (frequency separation for blemishes, unify face complexion to kill mixed-light casts, flyaway/hair cleanup) while preserving pore-level detail. Hand off as 16-bit ProPhoto RGB TIFF via the Evoto plugin. Do NOT change background color in Evoto. If a commercial invoice forces an Evoto background replace: cap opacity at 85% (let 15% of original light fall-off bleed through, no floating-sticker); luminosity-match the new background brightness to the original wall to kill halos; push the edge feather/blend slider +10 to +15 so color bleeds into fine hairs; pre-clean the edge in Lightroom Optics panel first (Remove Chromatic Aberration + Defringe purple/green) so Evoto's AI cuts cleaner. Batch: AI Color Match maps one fully-edited hero's color relationships across the whole session.
inputs_needed: 16-bit ProPhoto TIFF exported from Lightroom, Evoto with plugin
output_artifact: polished skin / batch-matched final images with intact pores and clean edges
when_to_use: final retouch pass after Lightroom color/depth is locked
when_not: do not use Evoto as the primary color physics or background-color engine

problem: sora 2 prompt structure, director level sora prompt, cinematic ai ad prompt, time coded shotlist
symptom: Sora 2 invents details you didn't want, weak lip-sync, inconsistent space across cuts
technique: Sora 2 long-prompt: Production Brief vs Time-Coded Shotlist
exact_steps: Sora 2 is a reasoning model: anything you don't specify it invents. Choose length by intent: short prompt = declare format+style upfront and let it interpret; long prompt = director control. PRODUCTION BRIEF (atmospheric single scene) blocks: Format & tone; Main subject(s); Wardrobe and props; Location & framing (anchor foreground/mid/background for spatial continuity); Lighting & palette; Continuity rules (weather/time-of-day held across cuts); Actions & camera beats (1-3 timed beats, each pairs ONE camera move + ONE subject action); Montage plan (cuts, inserts, transitions, pacing like 'three fast inserts then 0.5s hold'); Dialogue (own labeled block for accurate lip-sync); Sound & foley (micro-sounds: peel, snap, pour); Finish (film grain, halation, LUT intent, poster frame). TIME-CODED SHOTLIST (fast ads): Header 'An [N]-second [FORMAT] with [TRANSITIONS] and [CAMERA STYLE]' then bracketed beats [0-A s] OPEN, [A-B] TRANSITION, etc., each = SHOT SIZE+ANGLE + ACTION + CAMERA BEHAVIOR + CUT/TRANSITION + AUDIO. Duration guide: 4s about 2-3 beats, 8s about 5 beats, 12s about 6-7 beats. Safety: no realistic real-person faces in image-to-video (use stylized), no celebrity-lookalike wording, no protected IP.
inputs_needed: Concept; chosen method (brief or shotlist); optional reference image
output_artifact: Director-grade Sora 2 clip with controlled framing/dialogue/pacing
when_to_use: When you need precise directorial control over a Sora 2 scene or ad
when_not: Quick low-effort idea where short descriptive/directive prompt is enough

Download as .blend and open it (keep Blender open). 2) Give Claude project context: 'I'll import the character, you analyze the rig structure, I describe animations in natural language (wave/jump/slide) and you create them.' problem: blurry background portrait, depth of field, bokeh, make photo look professional, separate subject from background
symptom: Portraits look flat and amateur because the background is sharp and competes with the subject's face.
technique: Aperture-priority + max zoom for shallow DOF (the pro look)
exact_steps: 1) Put the camera in Aperture Priority mode. 2) Dial the f-stop to the SMALLEST number your lens allows (f/2.8, or f/3.5 if that is the lowest). 3) Zoom the lens to its MAXIMUM zoom / longest focal length. 4) Focus on the subject's face. Result: face is tack sharp, background is fully blown out and blurry. Phone equivalent: use the camera app's Portrait mode. The two levers that create the blur are the widest aperture plus the longest focal length, focused on the eyes.
inputs_needed: A camera with aperture priority (or phone with Portrait mode), a subject, a background with depth behind them
output_artifact: A portrait with a tack-sharp face and a fully defocused background
when_to_use: Any single-subject portrait where you want pro subject-background separation (Reset headshots, IG hero, dating/LinkedIn profile shots).
when_not: Group photos or environmental/scenic shots where you need front-to-back sharpness; very tight spaces where you cannot zoom in.
example_command: os_technique_cards solve "my portrait background is sharp and distracting, how do I blur it for the pro look"

problem: make body part look bigger or smaller, hide stomach in photo, slim waist with pose, what to push toward camera
symptom: Whatever is closest to the lens looks enlarged, so flat-on stances make hips/waist/midsection look heavy and shrink the face.
technique: Proximity rule: closest to lens = largest (push assets forward, push flaws back)
exact_steps: Core rule: the thing closest to the camera receives the most spotlight and looks LARGER; the thing farther away looks smaller. To slim the lower body: shift weight to the BACK leg so hips/waist kick AWAY from camera, then lean the chest TOWARD camera. The same subject can look ~half as wide hips-to-hips just by kicking hips back vs forward, with no change to lens or angle. To enlarge eyes in a headshot: have subject lean in and look up, or raise the camera angle so the eyes sit closer to the lens than the body. To show off a worked-out arm: bring it to the front / lean on it. Hand test to prove it: a hand by the face looks normal; pushed toward the lens it looks bigger than the face; pulled back it looks tiny.
inputs_needed: Subject, ability to direct weight shift and camera height
output_artifact: A flattering frame where the desired feature is emphasized and the unflattering area is minimized
when_to_use: Every portrait. First lever to reach for when a body area reads too heavy or a feature reads too small.
when_not: When you deliberately want a documentary/honest representation and not optical flattery.
example_command: os_technique_cards solve "how do I pose to make the waist look smaller and the face larger"

problem: double chin in photos, jawline, neck looks short, chin up selfie habit, define jaw
symptom: Subjects (used to high selfie angles) point their chin up, which collapses the neck and produces a double chin.
technique: Turtle / chin-forward-and-down to elongate neck and kill double chin
exact_steps: Tell the subject to 'turtle': push the forehead toward the camera and extend the neck OUT and slightly DOWN (not up). Cue: 'chin down... no, push your forehead to the camera and extend your neck.' It feels and looks awkward live, so dramatize it, then either relax it slightly down or crop the awkwardness out. From a slightly elevated camera angle the extended-neck looks natural while the double chin disappears. Selfie shortcut for the same effect: do a half-swallow (press tongue to roof of mouth) right before the shutter to tighten the neck and lift the jawline.
inputs_needed: Subject, photographer cue, slightly elevated camera angle
output_artifact: Headshot/portrait with an elongated neck and defined jawline, no double chin
when_to_use: Any headshot or upper-body portrait, especially for fuller-faced subjects or anyone prone to chin-up posture.
when_not: Full-length shots where the extended neck reads weird; when a low camera angle is locked (low angle worsens double chins).
example_command: os_technique_cards solve "client has a double chin in the headshot, how do I pose it out"

problem: pose women, S curve, contrapposto, make pose feminine, flatter female form, thin the legs
symptom: Square, feet-wide, symmetrical stances look cheery and childish, not elegant; everything reads wide.
technique: Build the S-curve (contrapposto) from the feet up
exact_steps: 1) Square the subject up, put ankles together. 2) Lift one heel (just the heel) to start thinning. 3) Collapse/bend that same knee inward, which thins that whole section and bends the straight line into an S. 4) Turn that hip subtly AWAY from camera to thin further. 5) Shift weight onto the back hip. The painting term is contrapposto: a slight S-curve through the body is what flatters most people. Rule of thumb for women full-length: if you can bend it, bend it; if you can curve it, curve it. To deepen: front leg forward and up on toe, then arch the lower back (cue 'stick your butt out' not 'stick your stomach out') to reveal the lower-back curve.
inputs_needed: Subject who can stand and shift weight; sometimes an apple box for the front foot
output_artifact: An elegant, curvy standing pose with weight shift and visible S-line
when_to_use: Standing female portraits (Reset, editorial), brides, seniors where elegance is the goal.
when_not: Masculine male posing (use the V instead); fully symmetrical/regimental looks done on purpose.
example_command: os_technique_cards solve "how do I build the S curve pose for a woman standing full length"
source_segment: Sal Cincotta, lines 444-507; full-length segment arch-the-back, lines ~13060-13080

problem: pose men, make man look masculine, broad shoulders, posing tips for men, avoid feminine pose
symptom: Men stand straight, flat-footed, hands over crotch with feet parted; the form reads boxy with no peaks and valleys (like the letter I).
technique: Create the masculine V and turn the body toward the light
exact_steps: 1) Posing starts from the feet: shake them out, bring feet together, then bend the knee CLOSEST to the camera and put all weight on the BACK leg. 2) Hang the body forward in a 'glorified slouch' and lean the chest toward camera, creating peaks and valleys (a V, not an I). 3) Turn the whole body TOWARD the light source (cue: 'pretend you're on a turntable, your feet and legs turn too') to make him look bigger and broader. 4) Give the hands a job: one or both hands in pockets (thumbs IN or fully out, never four fingers out, never frame the crotch). 5) Bring elbows out slightly for a gap/silhouette. Note: turning a man AWAY from the light (the female recipe) reads feminine and thin, so avoid unless intended.
inputs_needed: Subject, an identifiable directional light source (window, garage door, key light)
output_artifact: A masculine standing portrait with V-shape, broad chest/shoulders, and relaxed slouch
when_to_use: Male standing portraits, business/brand headshots for men, plus-size men (lean further forward + chin out).
when_not: Female posing (turn away from light instead); when an intentionally androgynous/feminine look is wanted.
example_command: os_technique_cards solve "how do I pose a man to look broad and masculine"

problem: run out of poses, how to never run out of poses, systematic posing, change pose quickly, posing framework
symptom: Photographer or subject freezes and repeats the same 2-3 poses; thinks a new pose must be a drastically different shape.
technique: Seven posing points + rotate-for-a-new-pose (Sue Bryce system)
exact_steps: Work bottom-up through the seven joints/zones: 1) FEET/ankles: feet together to shoulder-width to wider; and rotate the whole body a little (a tiny rotation = a brand-new pose). 2) KNEES: tippy-toe one foot to activate the knee, bring it in (smaller/daintier) or out (wider/bolder). 3) HIP: shift weight/balance onto one leg (like waiting for a bus) and kick the hip out (straight stick becomes an avocado curve). 4) SHOULDERS: forward (vulnerable), back (strong), or one down toward the chin (sassy). 5) ELBOWS/wrists: hand shapes (intermediate). 6) HANDS: if stuck, do what you do daily (fix glasses, jeans, hair). 7) HEAD/NECK: tilts and chin-around; even a small chin move is a new pose. Change the legs first, the nose/chin last. The big takeaway: when you run out, just rotate slightly.
inputs_needed: Subject, awareness of the seven zones
output_artifact: An expanded set of distinct frames generated by adjusting one joint at a time
when_to_use: Any session where you or the subject runs dry; training a non-model; pacing a high-volume shoot.
when_not: n/a (universal scaffolding); skip the verbal labels if they make the subject overthink.
example_command: os_technique_cards solve "I keep running out of poses on set, give me a system"
source_segment: David Saw, lines ~14328-14432 (the seven posing points)

problem: subject looks stiff, awkward poses, get natural expressions, model frozen, break set selfie poses
symptom: Non-models lock into stiff, repeated 'set' poses (head tilt, peace sign) and look frozen; static frames feel lifeless.
technique: Movement + burst + isolated micro-motions to get natural shapes and real expressions
exact_steps: 1) Raise frames-per-second to ~5-10 fps (burst). 2) Get the subject MOVING: walking, skipping, jumping, spinning, swaying side to side, rocking on heels. Build up walking to skipping to jumping. 3) Fire the burst as they shift weight onto the FRONT foot (that frame captures the movement). 4) Catch the real expression AFTER the motion (everyone laughs after skipping). For a controlled version, give ONE isolated micro-motion at a time then reset (face this corner and rotate to me; take a step back and walk through the mark). For the fake-walking pose: give a floor mark, keep stride wide, and have them look back as if their name was called. Movement also breaks ingrained selfie habits.
inputs_needed: Camera in burst/continuous mode, room to move, a floor mark for walking
output_artifact: A run of candid, dynamic frames with natural body language and genuine expression
when_to_use: Non-models, stiff subjects, energy/fashion shots, anyone who over-poses.
when_not: Locked compositions needing precise framing; very low light where burst rates / shutter cannot freeze motion cleanly.
example_command: os_technique_cards solve "my subject is stiff and the poses look frozen, how do I loosen them up"

problem: what to do with hands, awkward hands in photos, posing arms, thin the arms, hands look big
symptom: Subjects do not know what to do with their hands; arms pressed to the body look heavy; hands point at the crotch or look claw-like.
technique: Hand and arm placement: pockets, gaps, pull-back, soft fingers
exact_steps: Hands: give them a job. Pockets are the safety net: thumb in / hand halfway / fully in. For men in jeans use thumb-in; in dress pants the whole hand goes in; if the thumb is out, point it DOWN, never horizontal. Avoid four fingers out and avoid framing the crotch. Arms: keep them OFF the body (pressing creates mass) by creating a GAP between arm and torso so the waist shape reads; this also makes a flattering triangle of negative space. To slim a heavier arm, pull the elbow BACK behind the hip line so the back half hides and recedes. Do not press the arm against the body in profile; float the elbow slightly forward so the arm looks slimmer. Fingers: keep them soft and relaxed, slight bend in the elbow (no toy-soldier straight arms); show both hands (a hidden hand looks like a missing limb); offer one or several fingers loosely, wrists relaxed.
inputs_needed: Subject; ideally garments with pockets or belt loops
output_artifact: Natural, relaxed hand/arm placement with slimming gaps and soft fingers
when_to_use: Every portrait; especially nervous non-models and sleeveless/heavier-arm situations.
when_not: n/a; over-posing hands on a man can read feminine, so keep it subtle.
example_command: os_technique_cards solve "client doesn't know what to do with their hands and arms look heavy"
source_segment: Sal Cincotta arms, lines 510-637; Gerry Guinness hands, lines 2889-3076; Daria Kosa arms, lines 6400-6604

problem: arm looks like a nub, legs look short, foreshortening, flat feet boring pose, static rigid pose
symptom: Limbs aimed at the lens compress into stubs; flat-footed locked-knee stances look static and push the stomach forward; symmetrical pairs read rigid.
technique: Posing checklist: kill foreshortening, kill flat feet, stagger the levels
exact_steps: Run a mental checklist on every frame: 1) FORESHORTENING: any limb coming straight to/from the lens compresses and loses context (elbow toward camera = arm becomes a nub; knees/feet at camera in a seated shot = smooshed legs; fingers pointing at lens on a table). Fix by lowering the arm to the side, turning knees/feet to the side, or angling the appendage across the frame. 2) FLAT FEET: never both feet flat with knees locked (it pushes the stomach forward and is static). Get feet on different levels (bend a knee, toe up, apple box, a step) to introduce a curve and shift hips back/chest forward. 3) LEVELS: when there are two of anything (feet, knees, hands, elbows, shoulders), do NOT keep them even or doing the same thing; stagger them to make the pose dynamic. Also watch for MERGERS: check the silhouette has negative space so the body does not read as a blob.
inputs_needed: Subject; optional apple boxes/steps for level changes
output_artifact: A dynamic, elongated full-length pose free of compressed limbs and rigid symmetry
when_to_use: Full-length and seated portraits; any pose that feels boxy, short, or static.
when_not: When deliberate symmetry/foreshortening is the creative intent.
example_command: os_technique_cards solve "the full length pose looks stiff and the limbs look short, what's my checklist"
source_segment: Full-length segment, lines ~12780-13180 (foreshortening, flat feet, levels, mergers); Gerry Guinness foreshortening, lines ~3309-3340

problem: subject looks wide, full width experienced, turn body to slim, negative space, triangles in pose
symptom: Anything square to the camera is experienced at full width; subjects who do not want their full width seen still stand front-on.
technique: Put the body on an axis + add negative space and triangles
exact_steps: Anything square to the lens reads at its full width, so put the body on an AXIS: rotate to a diagonal, put weight on the back hip, rotate the front foot out, hands in pockets for a lean, relaxed line. Pose bottom-up (set body language first, then the face). Counterbalance width with NEGATIVE SPACE: when the viewer sees the boundary/gap, they read where the shape ends, so create gaps between arm and torso. Triangles are the most aesthetically appealing negative-space shape, so build triangles with the limbs. If a loose garment fills the gap, clamp it behind to restore the negative space. Anti-sink cue when they slump on the axis: 'pull up through the base of the spine, drop the shoulders, weight in the back hip.' Tighten the abdominal wall (feeling of a crunch), never 'suck in your stomach.'
inputs_needed: Subject; optional clamp for garments
output_artifact: A slimmer, intentional pose with the body on a diagonal and clean triangular negative space
when_to_use: Any subject self-conscious about width; editorial and business portraits where a lean line is wanted.
when_not: When you specifically want a powerful full-width, square-on, symmetrical look.
example_command: os_technique_cards solve "subject reads too wide front on, how do I slim with angle and negative space"

problem: short light vs broad light, make face look thinner or wider, light direction for posing, sculpt face with light
symptom: Subject turned the wrong way relative to the light looks flat, too wide, or too thin for their face/gender goal.
technique: Turn the face into short light (slim) or broad light (wider/masculine)
exact_steps: Identify where the light comes from FIRST. SHORT LIGHT: subject faces toward the light so the lit side of the face is the NARROWER side away from camera; this slims the face (good for women, thin/heavier subjects you want narrowed). BROAD LIGHT: turn so the broader, camera-side of the face is lit; this enlarges the face and reads more masculine (good for a thin man you want broader; risky for a large face/large guy whose head can then look gigantic). Match light direction to the posing goal: turning a man toward the light broadens him (masculine V); turning a woman away from the light slims her. Same logic sculpts dimension: side light shades one side of the face to create the 2D-to-3D shaded-apple effect.
inputs_needed: A directional light source (window, modifier, key light) and a subject who can rotate
output_artifact: A portrait where light direction reinforces the desired face width and dimension
when_to_use: Any portrait with directional light; deciding which way to turn the subject before shooting.
when_not: Flat/even lighting where there is no short vs broad side; honest documentary intent.
example_command: os_technique_cards solve "which way do I turn the subject into the light to slim or broaden the face"

problem: subject can't take direction, freeze up posing, give model a reference, relax client, mirror posing
symptom: Telling a subject 'left/right' confuses them; direct verbal posing makes them stiff and self-conscious.
technique: Show-don't-tell + mirroring + the relax-and-catch reset
exact_steps: 1) MIRROR: instead of saying turn left/right, demo the pose and have them copy you as if looking in a mirror (attach a bit of humor to disarm them). 2) SHOW-DON'T-TELL with references: pull portraits (Pinterest, Annie Leibovitz, Mark Seliger, movie posters) on a phone/iPad, say 'this is the kind of thing I'm thinking,' even set it on the floor in front of them; they mimic it, then naturally adjust into a better, more genuine pose. 3) RELAX-AND-CATCH: when out of ideas, say 'just relax a minute, I'm changing camera settings' (you are not), keep one eye on them, and when they slip into their natural posture say 'hold that' and shoot (works only once or twice per shoot). 4) Pre-shoot warm-up: run through the poses, read their shyness/outgoingness, and use mirroring so they learn to take instruction. 5) Slow down, chat, observe; the natural moments happen when you stop firing. 6) Do NOT manhandle the client; mirror and cue ('put your hand here') instead of physically moving them, and ask first if you must.
inputs_needed: Reference images on a phone/iPad; a tripod helps so you can shoot without recomposing; rapport
output_artifact: Relaxed, genuine frames from a subject who could not take abstract verbal direction
when_to_use: Non-models, nervous clients, kids, first-time subjects; the start of any session (warm-up).
when_not: Experienced models who pose better with freedom (let them freestyle instead).
example_command: os_technique_cards solve "my client can't take posing direction and freezes, how do I get natural shots"

problem: lens choice for groups, wide angle distorts faces, compression, focal length for family photos, heads small on ends
symptom: Wide lenses up close distort people on the ends (small heads, stretched features); shooting too close to any face distorts it.
technique: Back up and compress: long lens for groups and flattering portraits
exact_steps: For groups/families, back UP and shoot long (85mm, 100mm, up to 200mm) to compress the subjects and background; do not grab a wide lens just to fit everyone in. At 35mm or wider the people on the ends distort and their heads shrink on the sensor (use ~17-20mm only when you intentionally want to show the whole place as an art print, accepting tiny heads). For individuals: situate the camera FARTHER away and zoom in rather than getting close, because the lens distorts everything up close; keep the camera level and around shoulder height; avoid heavy tilt. Prime-lens discipline: know your focal lengths (e.g. 35 and 50) so you enter a session already knowing the shots each lens will give. iPhone fix for a bad angle after the fact: crop tool to Distortion modes to change the apparent shooting angle.
inputs_needed: A longer lens or zoom, room to step back, group or single subject
output_artifact: Group and portrait frames with natural proportions and compressed, flattering perspective
when_to_use: Family/group sessions, any portrait where you have space to back up; choosing a lens before shooting.
when_not: Tight rooms with no room to retreat; when an exaggerated wide environmental/fisheye look is the goal.
example_command: os_technique_cards solve "what focal length and distance for a flattering family group photo"
source_segment: Family posing lens-choice, lines ~8307-8395; Juliana camera-distance/distortion, lines ~11465-11494

problem: pose couples, couple kiss looks awkward, wedding couple poses, posing two people, variations couples
symptom: When told to 'kiss,' couples go nose-to-nose and pucker, which flattens both faces; couple poses feel repetitive.
technique: Almost-kiss + LASH variations for couples
exact_steps: ALMOST KISS: turn the person whose hair/makeup you want shown toward the camera and the other away; have them tilt heads, bring faces close, and SMILE close-up (it feels awkward but reads pretty), then let them actually kiss afterward without smudged noses. For same-sex couples, switch who turns which way between frames. LASH = the four variations you can run inside any couple pose (except back-to-back): L = Laugh (cue them to look at each other and laugh normally), A = Almost kiss, S = Smile (one at the other / one at camera, or a slay/look-off), H = Heads (foreheads together, head on shoulder, kiss the cheek). Lock the base pose and tell the couple to HOLD it (re-setting wastes seconds); unbutton a man's jacket button for arm poses (and only ever button the top button of a blazer).
inputs_needed: A couple, one base pose, a base location
output_artifact: A run of varied, flattering couple frames from a single base pose in minimal time
when_to_use: Engagement/wedding couples, any two-person shoot, time-pressured portrait windows.
when_not: Back-to-back compositions (LASH does not apply); single-subject work.
example_command: os_technique_cards solve "how do I pose a couple so the kiss isn't awkward and get variety fast"

problem: portrait lighting patterns, where to place the light, rembrandt loop split butterfly broad short
symptom: User doesn't know where to position a single light relative to the face to get a named, intentional look
technique: Nine-pattern clock placement system
exact_steps: Imagine a clock with the camera at 6 o'clock facing 12 and the subject in the center; place the light (flash or sun) at a clock hour. SPLIT: light at 9 or 3 (one side lit, one side shadow; harsh, shows wrinkles). BACKLIGHT/RIM: light at 12 behind subject. BUTTERFLY: light at 6, slightly above and in front (shadow under nose). CLAMSHELL: butterfly plus a reflector or fill light directly underneath. LOOP: main light just above eye level at 5 or 7 o'clock (small nose shadow, flatters most). REMBRANDT: light at 4 or 8 o'clock, far enough that the nose shadow joins the cheek shadow, leaving an upside-down triangle of light under the opposite eye. SHORT: like Rembrandt but turn the subject toward the light (slimming). BROAD: like Rembrandt but turn subject away from light (widens face). CROSS: main at 4-5 o'clock plus an edge light at 10-11 o'clock. Remember: the pattern is set by how the FACE relates to the light, not the body, so adjust by moving the chin.
app: Studio strobe / natural light (camera + single key light)
inputs_needed: One key light or sun, a subject, a camera position
output_artifact: A deliberately chosen, named lighting pattern on the subject's face
when_to_use: Pre-shoot lighting design, training, or diagnosing why a portrait looks flat or unflattering
when_not: Multi-light commercial sets where the pattern logic is overridden by product/edge lights

problem: flat butterfly loop rembrandt split lighting comparison, how each pattern looks on face and body
symptom: User wants to move a single light progressively through the five core patterns and know the purpose of each
technique: Five-pattern progressive light walk (flat to split)
exact_steps: Single light (e.g. Profoto B10) with an octabox on a rolling C-stand. Settings shown: 1/200, f/4, ISO 100. FLAT/DIRECT: light from the same angle as the lens (on- or off-camera); fills lines and blemishes, flattering, default for fashion/beauty. BUTTERFLY/PARAMOUNT: push the same light closer and raise it high; fills most shadow but adds a nose shadow. LOOP: bring the head down and rotate ~45 degrees off the camera axis; shadow on one side of nose and body. REMBRANDT: move the light further and deeper into the scene until, looking from the light, you can see the opposite cheek; gives the under-eye triangle and the most drama. SPLIT: light placed perpendicular (directly to the subject's side); splits both face and body. More shadow equals more drama. Control short vs broad by turning the chin toward the light (short, slimming, default) or away (broad, widens a narrow face).
inputs_needed: One strobe, octabox/scrim, rolling stand, camera
output_artifact: A side-by-side comparison set of the five portrait patterns
when_to_use: Learning or demonstrating the pattern continuum and choosing one by storytelling intent
when_not: When you need separation/edge or background light, which this single-light walk omits

problem: studio fashion editorial lighting setup, even overhead light plus key and rim, full body
symptom: User wants a repeatable high-fashion studio rig that lights a full scene evenly while making the model stand out
technique: Overhead silk bounce + octabox key + beauty-dish fill + hair light + negative fill
exact_steps: Build a 12x12 ft frame with a full-stop silk over the whole shooting area; point two strobe heads with reflectors UP into the silk so the light bounces back down evenly (bigger source relative to subject = softer). Boom a 3-foot octabox WITH a grid right in front of the model's face as the KEY. Add a beauty dish on a low stand on the floor as FILL for the legs/lower body and low catchlights. Behind the backdrop, add a 1x4 rectangular softbox with a grid pointing down as a subtle HAIR light on head and shoulders. Flank the model with two black polyboards (flags) for NEGATIVE FILL to deepen cheekbone shadows and add a back rim. Camera: Canon R5, 70-200mm f/2.8 for compression. Lower the overhead frame for floor/seated shots so the bounce still hits correctly.

problem: hard light saturated color fashion, gobo pattern on background, gel fill, three strobe setup
symptom: User wants a bold, high-contrast, color-saturated fashion frame with patterned background and colored shadows
technique: Three-strobe optical-spot setup with gobo background and gelled bounce fill
exact_steps: MAIN/KEY (camera left): Profoto D2 with a Westcott Optical Spot using the kit lens for crisp, very hard light that lights only the face/torso with sharp shadow edges (hard light saturates color but washes out makeup, so use heavy makeup). BACKGROUND: a second Optical Spot, swap the kit lens for a wider Canon 24-70 f/2.8 EF lens for more spread, and drop a gobo (a shape/texture pattern) into it to project slices of light/texture onto the backdrop. FILL: bounce a bare-bulb strobe off a white/neutral ceiling or wall to lift shadows across subject and background (avoid colored walls; higher ceilings give a more even spread); add a magenta/fuchsia gel to the fill so color shows up in the shadow areas. Shoot tethered into Capture One; if popping contrast darkens shadows, bump fill power.

inputs_needed: 2 optical spots (kit lens + EF zoom), gobo, bare-bulb strobe, magenta gel, white/neutral ceiling, tether + Capture One

problem: beauty lighting setup, soften octabox, negative fill contouring, background light bleed
symptom: User wants soft, contoured beauty light in a home/rental studio and controls for spill and shadow shaping
technique: Gridded octabox key softened with a diffusion panel, negative fill + bounce board control
exact_steps: Strobe settings: ISO 400, f/5.6, shutter 1/125 (shutter irrelevant with strobe). KEY: deep octabox (nicer round catchlights than a rectangular box) set high and angled down for flattering cheekbone gradient, with internal+external diffusion and a grid as a base. To SOFTEN further, remove the grid (pointless behind diffusion) and add a large diffusion frame in front (150x150 up to 4x4/6x6); bigger source = smoother falloff and a bigger panel catchlight. Below the face, raise/lower a white polyboard/foam BOUNCE BOARD to gently fill under the chin without an obvious bottom source. Place a BLACK poly flag on the opposite side as NEGATIVE FILL to carve cheekbone contour and stop spill past the model. BACKGROUND: a separate octa (e.g. Octa 120) lighting the backdrop; always test-shoot the background light alone to confirm its bleed isn't lifting your exposure. If the key gets too high, watch for shadow creeping into the eye socket, then add a front/below fill. Optionally push a beauty dish in toward the model to boost the makeup feel.

problem: rim light profile silhouette, no catchlight in eye, backlight portrait

exact_steps: Pose the subject in profile with the light source (large octabox) behind them at 12 o'clock and a black foam board between subject and the box; if the box is much larger than the card you'll usually get a catchlight. If you don't get one automatically: have the subject stand in profile facing your left, then turn their head slightly toward the light, then shift yourself slightly to your left to capture the silhouette with light on their eyelids. Mirror it for the other side (face right, turn slightly left, wiggle right).

Butterfly pushed closer and raised becomes Paramount, used historically for celebrity headshots.

problem: understand light quality strength direction, hard vs soft, front side back light
symptom: User can't reason about why a scene looks the way it does or how to change it without gear
technique: Three core light concepts + three shooting directions
exact_steps: Evaluate every light source on three axes: QUALITY (natural/sun is highest quality and gets soft; many artificial sources are low quality, e.g. flickering coffee-shop bulbs, and never fully mimic the sun); STRENGTH (strong source = hard, contrasty; weak source = soft, lower contrast; cameras capture ~13-15 stops of dynamic range vs the eye's ~21-24, so harsh light forces you to choose highlights or shadows); DIRECTION (the biggest lever). Then pick a direction: FRONT light (light behind you) = even exposure but flat, few shadows; SIDE light = beautiful shadows, depth, the default to reach for; BACK light = deepest/darkest shadows and drama, risks silhouette if too strong. Shift your own perspective relative to subject and source to change direction without moving lights. Modify with a softbox (artificial) or 5-in-1 reflector (reflect or diffuse through a white sheet); use smoke/haze/mist for atmospheric rays; white surfaces bounce soft light, black cards/walls absorb to deepen shadows.
inputs_needed: A subject, awareness of the source, optionally a reflector/diffuser or flag
output_artifact: A deliberate quality+strength+direction decision for the shot
when_to_use: Foundational lighting decisions on location or when teaching the basics
when_not: When a fixed multi-light studio recipe already dictates placement
example_command: os_technique_cards solve "reason about light quality strength and direction for a portrait"

problem: best time of day to shoot, golden hour blue hour midday overcast, natural light planning
symptom: User doesn't know which natural-light window fits the look they want
technique: Four natural-light windows + shoot-into-shadows discipline
exact_steps: GOLDEN HOUR (sunrise/sunset): soft directional side light, low contrast, easiest for the sensor; note sunrise vs sunset put the sun in different parts of the sky, so a scene backlit at sunrise may be front-lit at sunset (use Photo Pills to predict the sun's position). BLUE HOUR (~1 hr before sunrise / after sunset): very soft with a blue tint, dreamy/moody, but dark, so open up the aperture (e.g. f/1.4). MIDDAY/HARD LIGHT: fine for cities (tall buildings cut hard light into geometric lines, leading lines, deep shadows); bad for foliage/nature (hot spots on leaves); wait ~2 hours off noon for softer angles. OVERCAST: clouds diffuse the sun into soft even light, great for portraits and even face exposure. Core discipline: you can't change light after capture, so get it right in camera; SHOOT INTO THE SHADOWS (side/back light) instead of front light for depth; treat light itself as a possible subject; shift perspective to rescue bad light.
app: Natural light (camera, optional Photo Pills app)
inputs_needed: Location, time-of-day plan, camera, optional 5-in-1 reflector
output_artifact: A natural-light shooting plan matched to the desired mood
when_to_use: Planning outdoor/location shoots and choosing the shooting window
when_not: Controlled studio strobe work where ambient timing is irrelevant

problem: hard vs soft light control, inverse square law falloff, why far light still soft in small room
symptom: User can't predict shadow hardness/falloff or why a distant light looks low-contrast indoors
technique: Apparent-size hard/soft control + inverse square law
exact_steps: Hardness depends on the light's APPARENT SIZE from the subject's view: a large source close = soft, big, low-texture; a small source (or any source far away, since distance shrinks apparent size) = hard, more texture, harsher specular highlights. Closer light = bigger = softer; further = smaller = harder. INVERSE SQUARE LAW: light falls off faster the closer it is to the subject (quick intensity drop over a given distance) and more gradually when far. Counterintuitive trap: in a confined/small studio a far light should be harder, but more of its light bounces off walls and fills the shadows, so the image actually reads LOWER contrast. To raise contrast in a small space, flag the bounce with black polys/cards; to soften, enlarge the source or bring it closer. Also control: position (front = less shadow/texture; side/low = more; below = unsettling/horror feel) and color (kelvin/white balance, full vs low spectrum). Modifiers must be used at appropriate distance, not too far.
inputs_needed: A controllable light, modifiers, black flags, knowledge of room size
output_artifact: Predictable shadow hardness and contrast control
when_to_use: Diagnosing or designing contrast and falloff, especially in small spaces
when_not: When you simply want to follow a fixed recipe without tuning falloff
example_command: os_technique_cards solve "control hard vs soft light and inverse square falloff in a small studio"

problem: fill shadows on subject and background at once, colored shadows, bounce fill

Requirements: white/light-gray/neutral walls only (green/orange walls cast color onto the subject); higher ceilings give a more even spread, low ceilings still work but less evenly. To add color into the shadows, gel the fill (e.g. magenta) since gels show up most in shadow areas; this pushes color further into the frame. Shoot a no-modifier test first, then add creative tweaks.

problem: how to make a moodboard for a photo shoot, fashion shoot moodboard sections, communicate vision to crew

Sections do NOT need to share one color palette; each section carries its own intention. 4) Model section = emotion, movement, expressions, body lines (e.g. elongated limbs, looseness). 5) Lighting section = mood from a lighting POV (e.g. deep dark shadows, key features lit, one-light from one direction). 6) Location/Set = the space PLUS props/relevant elements. 7) Hair & Makeup = be hyper-specific (call out lips vs eyes separately, e.g. silver on eyes, natural lips) so the MUA does not guess from a whole face. 8) Wardrobe = silhouette intent (e.g. clean simple silhouette so it does not compete with movement). 9) Add short notes + arrows next to images ('we want the idea of the model consumed by the material, not this color').

Page 5 VIBES: header 'Vibes' + photos that capture the overall energy/personality. Put your NAME + WEBSITE + 'a creative concept by [you]' on EVERY page (not just front/back) to prevent idea theft. Use on set: print 3 hard copies (hair/makeup station, wardrobe room, near your lenses/lights) as live reminders; also hand to your editor in post so they match the approved plan.

problem: reusable Photoshop moodboard template, grid moodboard fast, quick printable shoot board
symptom: Photoshop grid does not match the ruler; images do not snap cleanly; rebuilding the layout every time is slow
technique: Reusable A4 percentage-grid template + masked-box collage in Photoshop
exact_steps: 1) File > New > document type International Paper (A4). 2) View > Rulers and View > Show > Grid. 3) Right-click ruler > set to Percent. 4) Edit > Preferences > Guides, Grid & Slices: set gridline every 10 with 4 subdivisions (line every 2.5%) so grid matches the percentage ruler. 5) View > Snap and Snap To > Grid + Guides on. (Snap may only catch vertical lines; pull horizontal guides from the top ruler at 10%, 20%, etc., grabbing with the Move tool.) 6) Draw boxes: rectangle + new layer + paint bucket; duplicate (Cmd/Ctrl+J), move, Free Transform (Cmd/Ctrl+T) into varied sizes leaving 1-cell gaps. 7) Merge all box layers (select top, shift+select bottom, Ctrl/Cmd+E). 8) Ctrl/Cmd-click the merged layer to load selection, new layer, Select > Inverse, fill the surround gray (later white) = the mask/template. SAVE this as a reusable template. To build a board: Google Images > advanced search > image size larger than 400x300; right-click 'open image in new tab' then copy; paste each into PS; drag/Free Transform images into boxes (overlap is fine), then select each box layer and delete bleed. Set the top template layer's Color Overlay to Normal (turns white) so it can be toggled. File > Print on A4. Build a separate B&W 'shape board' of poses (add Hue/Sat adjustment layer desaturated + a Curves layer adding blacks/whites to emphasize shapes).

problem: make AI generated set look real, composite AI background into real studio, blend AI image with real photo, AI set looks fake
symptom: A fully AI-generated set looks synthetic and does not match the real studio space; client/audience can tell it is AI.
technique: 3-Layer Studio-DNA Stitching
exact_steps: Layer 1 (Base): place the generated AI set as the bottom environment layer, using it only for overall lighting, color reference, and the back halo/spotlight. Layer 2 (Realism Overlays): overlay high-res photos of your OWN studio textures (concrete floor texture, industrial window-frame shapes) onto the EDGES of the frame; keep the AI center clean, mask the overlays so the real texture only appears at frame edges, feather/blend the mask so there is no hard seam. Layer 3 (Brand/Prop Anchor): composite the real product/prop onto the set; match its perspective to the scene and add it on its own layer for shadow control. Goal: AI center + real studio edges = looks photographed in the actual space.

problem: composited object looks flat, prop looks like a sticker, pasted object not grounded, add contact shadow
symptom: A composited book/prop or subject looks pasted-on and flat; no shadow where it touches the surface, lighting on it does not match the room.
technique: Contact-Shadow Grounding Pass
exact_steps: 1. Add proper CONTACT shadows directly underneath the object where it physically touches the surface (stool/floor): paint a soft dark shadow on a Multiply layer, darkest at the contact point, fading outward. 2. Match the object's cover/surface lighting to the room's light source direction and warmth (dodge/burn or a clipped curves/levels layer to align highlights and shadows with the scene). 3. For a SUBJECT composited onto a seat: show weight, the seat cushion compresses slightly under them, and add realistic drop shadows on the seat, legs, and floor so they are physically anchored. 4. Soften the transition line where a backdrop meets the floor and add a subtle resting shadow so the backdrop looks like it sits on the ground.

output_artifact: Grounded composite where the object reads as a physical object in the space

problem: kling multi-shot, multiple camera angles one generation, ai video keeps cutting wrong, build a story longer than 3 seconds in kling
symptom: Single-prompt Kling clips are one continuous shot; cannot get cuts between angles or a narrative inside one 15s generation; scenes drift.

exact_steps: In Kling 3.0 (via Higgsfield), toggle Multi-Shot mode ON. Break the 15-second block into up to 6 distinct shots, each 2s-4s minimum (3s is the working unit). Write one independent prompt per shot block defining camera move + action. Keep each prompt under 500 characters. Plan the transition inside the prompt itself (end a sentence/action in one shot to trigger the cut to the next location). Run the full sequence as one 15s generation so cuts and consistency are native, not stitched in post.

exact_steps: Generate two stills: a clean version (no text) and a final version (with text/graphics). Set length 5-6s. Kling interpolates from start to end, producing the animated reveal. Reverse the order to animate text out. Use bridge-frame chaining: set the END frame of clip A as the START frame of clip B for seamless scene links.

symptom: Natural-language descriptions produce inconsistent lighting/pose/composition; the model ignores instructions.
technique: LLM meta-prompting for Kling shots
exact_steps: Do not freehand the Kling prompt. problem: 15 second cinematic sequence, multiple shots one generation, multi character dialogue lip sync, kling 3.0
symptom: Building a multi-shot narrative by stitching single clips is slow and breaks continuity.

problem: cold email deliverability, landing in spam, domain setup, how many emails per inbox, warm up
symptom: emails land in spam, main domain reputation burned, open rates near zero
technique: Decoupled Multi-Domain Sending Infrastructure
exact_steps: Never send volume from your primary brand domain. Buy multiple lookalike domains (e.g. .info/.co/.com variations) at Porkbun; for high scale, attach several inbox accounts per domain (commonly 3-5 per domain; aggressive operators run far more). Set SPF, DKIM, and DMARC DNS records on every domain (Instantly tests these and gives a guide if any fail). Cap sending at ~30 emails/inbox/day to stay under the spam radar; for brand-new domains start at 1-5/day and ramp slowly. Warm up every inbox for 2-3 weeks before outreach (Instantly warm-up + read-emulation; do not disable slow warm-up). Use a ~70/30 Outlook/Google split and provider-match send (Gmail-to-Gmail) to spread risk. Verify every email (Million Verifier / in-platform) to keep bounces near zero. Disable open/click tracking to protect IP reputation. Monitor each account's health score and pause any below ~85 to warm-up only.

problem: automate brand identity, generate logo color palette fonts mockups, AI brand identity workflow, deliver brand without a designer
symptom: Need to produce logos, color palettes, fonts, and product mockups fast from just a business name and description, without spending hours in Canva or hiring a designer.

exact_steps: Build this n8n workflow: 1) FORM TRIGGER with two fields: company name, short description. 2) LLM node (Claude via OpenRouter, or ChatGPT/Gemini) with system prompt: 'You are a lead brand identity designer specializing in modern flat design and minimalism. problem: key fill rim light setup, how to place three lights portrait, what is rim light, three light rig
symptom: portrait looks flat, subject blends into background, no separation, no professional modeling on the face
technique: Three-Light Functions (Key / Fill / Rim)
exact_steps: KEY: one key per setup, place to the side of the subject, above eye level, angled down so the shadow under the nose falls onto the cheek (not onto the upper lip). FILL: weaker than key, fills the shadow side so it does not go solid black; set the ratio deliberately (low fill = dramatic, high fill = commercial/clean); adjust via distance, power, or a reflector instead of adding a second strobe. RIM: place behind and slightly above the subject to create a highlight along hair/shoulders; use a grid or a strip softbox with a honeycomb to keep the rim out of the lens. Rim light is the fastest way to make a portrait read as professional.
inputs_needed: Subject, key light source, fill (reflector or weaker softbox), rim light (strip softbox + grid), light stands

when_not: Run-and-gun natural light, documentary work, or when only window light is available

problem: hard light vs soft light, how to make light softer, shadow edges too sharp, light too harsh
symptom: shadows are too sharp/too soft for the look, skin texture too revealing or too flat, wrong contrast for the genre
technique: Hard vs Soft Light Control by Source Size + Distance
exact_steps: Hard light = small source relative to subject (sharp shadow edges, reveals skin texture, shiny highlights; for fashion/editorial/contrast). Soft light = large source relative to subject (gradient shadow edges, smooths skin, lower contrast; for beauty/commercial). To change hardness without changing lights: move the light CLOSER to make it softer, FARTHER to make it harder. Or add a diffusion panel (softer) / remove one (harder). Or swap modifiers: bare strobe = hard, same strobe through an octabox = soft, same octabox with a grid = directional soft.
inputs_needed: Light source, optional diffusion panel/modifiers, space to move the light
output_artifact: Light quality matched to the genre (fashion contrast vs beauty smoothness)
when_to_use: First decision in any lighting setup; whenever shadow quality does not match the intended look

problem: which light modifier to use, softbox vs beauty dish vs strip, what does a grid do, negative fill
symptom: owning too many or wrong modifiers, catchlights wrong, light spilling everywhere, shadow side too flat
technique: Working Modifier Set for Portrait/Commercial
exact_steps: Octabox/softbox: large soft directional source, octa gives circular catchlights; use as the DEFAULT key (90% of pro portrait work). Beauty dish: medium-hard directional, place above and angled down for the characteristic shadow under the cheekbone; beauty/fashion. Strip softbox: long narrow source for elongated highlights; use for rim lights and fashion profiles, add a grid to stop lens flare. Diffusion panel: scatter any source through translucent material to soften (window through a bedsheet, strobe through a scrim). Grid/honeycomb: narrows the beam, reduces spill, concentrates light into a pocket. Reflector (physical): bounces existing light as fill for outdoor/low-budget. Negative fill (poly board): absorbs light on the shadow side to DEEPEN the shadow when the face looks flat; essential for dramatic commercial.

output_artifact: Correct modifier choice per shot intent

problem: what grid degree to use, how to stop rim flaring lens, spotlight effect with grid, narrow beam light
symptom: rim light flaring into the lens, light spilling onto the background, cannot isolate a pocket of light
technique: Grid Degree Selection + Placement
exact_steps: Grids are rated 5, 15, 30, 45 degrees: smaller number = narrower beam = tighter light pocket. A 5-degree grid on a zoom reflector = a spotlight you can place precisely on one area of the face or set. Put a grid on rim lights to keep them from flaring the lens (if you have never done this, add one next shoot and compare). Put a grid on the key to create rapid falloff from lit to unlit so the face is bright while the background goes completely dark. For hard-light fashion, use a 15-degree grid on a zoom reflector or bare strobe as a hard key.

problem: short lighting vs broad lighting, make face look narrower or wider, which side of face to light
symptom: face reads too wide/too narrow, modeling does not flatter the subject's face shape
technique: Short vs Broad Lighting Decision
exact_steps: SHORT lighting: the side of the face facing AWAY from camera is lit, the side facing camera is in shadow; makes the face look narrower and more sculpted. BROAD lighting: the side of the face facing the camera is lit, the other side in shadow; makes the face look wider and larger. Control which side is lit by the angle between the key and the face relative to the camera: the light setup stays put, the SUBJECT turns the face toward or away from the key. Portrait rule of thumb: short lighting on rounder faces, broad on thinner faces. Commercial rule of thumb: short for drama/style, broad for approachability/warmth.

problem: expose for skin tone, darker skin underexposed, blown highlights light skin, meter the face, spot metering portrait
symptom: darker skin fades into background, lighter skin blows out on forehead/nose, camera averages the exposure wrong
technique: Meter for the Face (Skin-Tone Exposure Discipline)
exact_steps: Spot meter on the FACE, not the averaged frame. Darker skin tones: find the light, commit to the exposure, do not underexpose to protect other highlights; meter for the face and add +2/3 to +1 full stop of exposure compensation (the in-camera meter underexposes darker skin). Lighter skin tones: meter for the highlights, pull down or diffuse the key, subtract -2/3 to -1 stop so skin texture holds at the cost of a slightly darker shadow side. For a subject backlit by bright sky (camera silhouettes them): add light to the face (flash/reflector/closer brighter key) OR move the subject so light is on the face. Protect the face; let other highlights resolve in post.
inputs_needed: Camera with spot meter + exposure compensation, the subject's face
output_artifact: Correctly exposed face regardless of background brightness
when_to_use: Every portrait, especially mixed/backlit light and across a range of skin tones
when_not: Stylized intentional silhouettes where the face is meant to be dark

problem: blurry background portrait, shallow depth of field settings, aperture for bokeh, professional blur
symptom: background too sharp/distracting, portrait does not read professional, no subject separation via blur
technique: Background Blur Camera Settings
exact_steps: Use Aperture Priority mode. Set the smallest f-number your lens allows (f/2.8, f/1.8, f/1.4): smaller number = shallower depth of field. Zoom to the LONGER end of your lens (longer focal length compresses and blurs the background further). Focus on the eyes, specifically the NEAR eye (not the bridge of the nose, not the cheek). On a phone, use Portrait mode. These four steps produce the professional blurred-background look before any other decision matters.
inputs_needed: Camera with aperture priority + a fast lens, or a phone with Portrait mode
output_artifact: Portrait with a clean, blurred, compressed background

when_not: Environmental portraits where the setting must stay sharp; group shots needing depth

problem: where to place subject on location, on-location workflow order, chasing light and background problems
symptom: constantly fighting light and background issues that the pose cannot fix, posing before checking light
technique: Light / Location / Layout Sequence
exact_steps: Run this strict 3-step sequence on every new spot within a location. 1) LIGHT first: find where the sun is, where your shadow is, where bounce/fill comes from; place the subject so light lands on the face without being blown out or lost in shadow. 2) LOCATION second: check the background behind the subject for dark holes, busy distractions, or clipping elements behind the head; adjust your angle or the subject's position until the background is clean. 3) LAYOUT last: only now pose the subject, using the composition and lighting to advantage instead of fighting them. Never start with layout, that forces you to chase light/background problems the pose cannot fix.
inputs_needed: Location, subject, awareness of sun/shadow/bounce surfaces
output_artifact: A frame where light, background, and pose all serve the image (in that priority)
when_to_use: Every new spot on every location shoot
when_not: Fully pre-lit studio where light and background are already locked
example_command: os_technique_cards solve "what order do I work a location spot"

problem: how to pose a subject, generate poses fast, run out of poses, posing vocabulary, male and female default pose
symptom: subject poses stiff/awkward, photographer freezes on what to pose next, men cross hands over crotch, women stand square and stiff
technique: Seven Posing Points + Male/Female Defaults + Rotation Trick
exact_steps: Treat a pose as 7 independent levers; adjust ONE at a time, leave the other six, the pose changes each time (cycle all seven in a 2-minute session for ~20 frames). 1) Feet: planted wide/together/tiptoe, rotated in/out. 2) Knee: bending the FRONT knee is the most reliable small-change move. 3) Hip: shift weight onto one leg for the natural waiting-for-a-bus stance. 4) Torso: slight forward lean (glorified slouch) brings chest/shoulders forward, pushes gut away. 5) Shoulders: square=confrontational, angled=at ease, turned=profile/elegant. 6) Arms/hands: men=hands in pockets (thumbs IN, fingers outside the pant); women=one hand at collar/waist/hair. 7) Head/eyes: chin slightly down and forward to reduce double chin, nose toward the light, eyes to lens for connection or past it for mood. MALE recovery: turn whole body toward the light, hands in pockets (thumbs in), feet close, bend front knee, slight forward lean, chin forward+down. FEMALE recovery: shift weight to one leg, resting leg on tiptoe/bent, one hand to a body point, angle shoulders off square, chin down + nose to light, commit the eyes. ROTATION TRICK: when out of poses, rotate the subject; 45 deg = a new pose, 90 deg = another, back-to-camera with torso twisted = another.
inputs_needed: Subject in frame, a light source to turn toward
output_artifact: A repeatable pose vocabulary generating many usable frames from one starting pose
when_to_use: Every portrait session; especially untrained subjects and when poses run dry
when_not: Fast candid/documentary capture where directing would break the moment
example_command: os_technique_cards solve "recover an untrained male subject standing square"

problem: how to build a moodboard, moodboard structure for a shoot, pinterest graveyard, brief the team and client
symptom: team shows up in different aesthetic directions, board is 30 disagreeing images, client unsure photographer can deliver
technique: Five-Page Moodboard + Working Discipline
exact_steps: Build exactly 3-5 pages (do not skip, do not add more). Page 1 Title image: one hero that makes the client think 'this is the photographer' (single most important page). Page 2 Tone: 3-5 images setting emotional register (warmth/tension/formality/playfulness). Page 3 Hair, makeup, styling: two images per bucket chosen for CONSISTENCY not variety. Page 4 Lighting reference: 3-5 images showing the SAME lighting direction, quality, and contrast (the team's technical brief). Page 5 Location reference: 2-4 images of the space type or the actual scouted location. Discipline: one secret board per project named for the shoot (not a mega-board); remove any image that conflicts with the direction even if you like it; lock the board before outreach. AI diagnostic: drive a reference render with a void prompt (just a pair of quotation marks) to see what the board produces stylistically independent of subject. In Midjourney, control board influence with stylize value (default 100; drop toward 15-50 if output clones the board; up to 1000 forces near-total adherence) and run style raw in parallel as a second draft. Deliver three versions: 3-5pg PDF/link to client; condensed 2-3pg (title/tone/styling/outfit, no lighting brief) to model; full board + call sheet to team, before the shoot with more than one day lead.
inputs_needed: Source images, a layout tool (Milanote), shoot concept; optionally Midjourney for reference renders
output_artifact: A locked 5-page visual brief delivered in client/model/team versions
when_to_use: Before every shoot, before any model/stylist outreach
when_not: Never skip; even a compressed shoot gets a compressed (still 5-page) board
example_command: os_technique_cards solve "build a 5-page moodboard that aligns the team"

problem: how to validate offer before building / will this sell / test demand first
symptom: Tempted to spend weeks/months building a product before confirming anyone wants it; fear of launching to silence
technique: Rule One: Validate before you build (organic demand first, inventory second)
exact_steps: Before building anything, run cheap validation that returns signal within ONE week: (1) post a mockup on social, (2) gift samples to 10-20 small creators, (3) write 3 Medium articles on the topic, (4) search Amazon for competing books and read the 1-star reviews. Strong signals = fit, begin production. Weak signals = offer not right yet, do not build. Never mass-produce or write the full product before proof of demand exists.

problem: how to research a niche / is there a market / validate niche demand
symptom: Have an offer idea but no evidence the market wants it; guessing instead of measuring
technique: The Four Validation Methods (Amazon / Medium / Reddit / Competitor mining)
exact_steps: Run all four within 3-5 days. (1) AMAZON: find top 5 best-sellers in niche (published last 3 yrs, 100+ reviews), read every 1-star and 2-star review, compile complaints = product roadmap. (2) MEDIUM: if 20+ articles exist with 200+ claps each, interest is proven; write 3 articles 1-2 weeks apart, measure reads/claps/signups. (3) REDDIT: search 'how to [topic]', count threads asking your exact question, note the exact language people use = your sales-page copy. (4) COMPETITOR: find 5 best-sellers on Gumroad/Etsy/KDP, read every testimonial + negative review, buy 2-3 closest, list the gaps. Verdict: strong signal across all four = build; mixed = refine angle, revalidate 2 days; weak = kill and return to the three questions.
inputs_needed: Niche topic, access to Amazon/Medium/Reddit/competitor marketplaces
output_artifact: Validation report with complaint list, copy language bank, and go/refine/kill verdict

problem: how to niche down / my offer is too broad / who is this for
symptom: Targeting a broad category, low conversion, lost in a sea of competitors, audience does not feel spoken to
technique: The Third Layer Rule
exact_steps: Do not target the broad category (Layer 1: 'Fitness' = millions of competitors). Do not target the first subcategory (Layer 2: 'Running' = thousands, low conversion). Target the THIRD layer down (Layer 3: 'Knee pain for marathoners over 50' = few competitors, high conversion). Narrow until the buyer is specific and competition is low. Broad is a graveyard; narrow is a gold mine. The narrower the offer, the easier to validate, build, and sell.
inputs_needed: Current niche/category definition
output_artifact: A third-layer niche statement (specific intersection of audience + problem)
when_to_use: When defining or refining who an offer is for, or when conversion is low
when_not: When the niche is already at the third layer and converting

problem: how to price / what to charge / build an offer ladder / where to start pricing
symptom: Single-product business, no ascension path, or starting too high (2k coaching with no audience) or too low (7-dollar ebooks forever)
technique: The Six-Rung Offer Ladder + Start-One-Rung-Above rule
exact_steps: Six rungs, each qualifies the buyer for the next: (1) Free lead magnet ($0, email capture), (2) Low-ticket tripwire ($7-27, converts free to paid), (3) Mid-ticket ($27-97, primary revenue), (4) Video course ($97-497, authority), (5) Coaching/consulting ($500-5,000+, highest margin), (6) Done-for-you service ($1,000-20,000+, backend). PLACEMENT RULE: start ONE rung above your highest proven sale, not three. If you have never sold anything, start with free magnet + $7-27 tripwire. Under 10 copies sold = stay low-ticket and iterate. 100+ copies + 500+ engaged subscribers = build mid-ticket. Mid-ticket consistent + 2,000+ subscribers = build the $297-497 course. Coaching/DFY only after testimonials from lower rungs. NOTE: SNIPED Reset floor holds at $1,500; trade scope not price.
inputs_needed: Current highest proven offer + price, audience size, copies sold to date
output_artifact: A populated pricing ladder with the next 1-2 planned rungs
when_to_use: When deciding what to charge, what to launch next, or how to structure an ascension path
when_not: Do not plan more than two rungs ahead of current proven rung

problem: how to make an offer that sells / should I make it bigger or prettier
symptom: Building the prettiest/most comprehensive product instead of the one that removes a specific pain; over-polishing
technique: Rule Two: Utility beats aesthetics (specific problem, specific outcome)
exact_steps: Solve ONE specific recurring pain with a specific outcome. A 10-page PDF that makes one problem go away outsells a 200-page ebook covering everything. A simple template outsells a beautiful course. The buyer pays for the absence of the pain, not the product. Practical utility beats premium aesthetics at every price point BELOW $500. Above $500, utility remains necessary but brand identity becomes the differentiator that justifies price. Cover/title communicates the transformation, not the topic ('From Stuck at 10k to Consistent 50k Months' beats 'A Guide to Business Growth').
inputs_needed: Offer concept, target pain point, price point
output_artifact: A tightened offer scoped to one specific problem and outcome
when_to_use: When scoping an offer or deciding how much to build
when_not: Above $500 where brand identity must also carry weight (still keep utility)

problem: how to write a sales page / sales copy framework / cold copy
symptom: Sales page reads generic or AI-written; traffic scattered; conversion low
technique: PAS sales-page framework + The Rule of One
exact_steps: SALES PAGE uses PAS: (1) PROBLEM: state the specific problem in the buyer's exact language (pulled from Reddit/Medium research). (2) AGITATE: describe what happens if unsolved (cost, frustration, recurring pain). (3) SOLVE: introduce the offer as the specific mechanism that removes the pain. AI drafts first pass; you edit for voice and specificity; NEVER publish a first-draft AI sales page (the market can smell it). RULE OF ONE: one offer (no 3 products in one launch), one buyer (write to a single named person), one page (funnel all traffic to one sales page), one channel (pick the one matching your strength, ignore the rest until it works).
inputs_needed: Validated pain points, buyer's exact language from research, the offer
output_artifact: A PAS-structured sales page draft focused on one offer/buyer/page/channel
when_to_use: When writing or auditing a sales page or any conversion copy
when_not: When the page already converts and tests show no dilution
example_command: os_technique_cards solve "write the sales page for this offer"

problem: how to position an AI service / cold dm for service / service offer framing
symptom: Pitching 'AI services' or features; buyers discount the phrase; service reads as commodity
technique: Sell outcomes, not AI (feature framing to outcome framing)
exact_steps: Never sell 'AI' (commodity word, already discounted by buyers). Sell the specific outcome they cannot produce themselves. Convert features to outcomes: 'I implement an AI chatbot' becomes 'I build a system that answers customer inquiries 24/7 and books appointments while you sleep.' 'I set up AI automation' becomes 'I remove the manual work of sorting/tagging/routing leads so sales only sees qualified opportunities.' 'We do AI consulting' becomes 'We identify the 3 highest-leverage places AI saves you 20+ hours/week, then build those systems.' Every service pitch leads with the time saved or revenue produced, not the tool. SNIPED lock: faceless-safe, no identity exposure; no outreach executed by the OS.
inputs_needed: The service capability, target buyer's manual pain, measurable outcome
output_artifact: An outcome-framed service pitch line (draft only, not sent)
when_to_use: When framing or pitching any service/agency offer, or drafting service outreach
when_not: When selling a self-serve product where the deliverable speaks for itself
