problem: good fit client vs bad fit / when to productize / custom vs packaged service
symptom: Every engagement is custom, margin destroyed, business cannot scale; or productizing before the pattern is clear
technique: The Lego-Brick model + Productize-at-3 rule
exact_steps: Do not start a full-service agency. (1) Identify ONE high-value repeatable problem in ONE specific industry. (2) Build it for one client at cost or below, with explicit agreement the work becomes a case study. (3) Document the system, record implementation, capture measurable outcome. (4) Package as a productized service: fixed scope, fixed timeline, fixed price. (5) Sell the same package to the next 10 clients in the same industry; delivery cost drops sharply. (6) Add a second module only after the first has 10-25 clients and repeat-delivery economics. PRODUCTIZE-AT-3: productize as soon as the same requirement appears across 3+ clients. Keep first 2-3 engagements custom on purpose to see what repeats. Maintain a custom tier ABOVE the productized tier at 2-3x the productized price for buyers who will not fit a box.
inputs_needed: Target industry, the repeatable problem, current client requirements list
output_artifact: A productized service spec (fixed scope/timeline/price) + custom-tier price
when_to_use: When deciding whether to keep a service custom or package it, or which clients fit
when_not: Before you have run 2-3 engagements and seen the repeating pattern
example_command: os_technique_cards solve "should I productize this service or keep it custom"

problem: how to build a brand / brand foundation / who is the enemy / brand positioning
symptom: Starting with logo/visuals before strategy; pretty work that does not sell; brand has no edge
technique: The Five Foundational Brand Questions (design comes last)
exact_steps: Answer in full sentences BEFORE any pixel, name, or logo: (1) WHO IS THIS FOR: psychographics not demographics ('6ft+ women who can never find pants that fit' is a brand; 'Women 25-35' is useless). (2) WHAT PROBLEM DOES THIS SOLVE: in the buyer's own language, not the maker's. (3) WHAT DO YOU STAND FOR: including what you refuse to do (strong brands have strong refusals). (4) WHAT GUT FEELING: exactly three adjectives, no more. (5) WHO IS THE ENEMY: the industry pattern/incumbent behavior you fight against (e.g. 'faceless digital products that read like AI vomit'). BRAND GAP TEST: survey 10 people for three words describing your brand, compare to your internal five answers; the distance is your brand gap, close it operationally.
inputs_needed: Target buyer, the problem, brand values, category incumbents
output_artifact: Completed five-question brand foundation doc + three-word gut-feeling set
when_to_use: Before any naming, logo, or visual work, or when a brand lacks edge
when_not: After the foundation is locked and visuals are already expressing it
example_command: os_technique_cards solve "build the brand foundation before design"

problem: how to launch / launch sequence / build anticipation / drop strategy
symptom: Surprise launches that under-convert; launching to existing followers instead of an owned list; no anticipation
technique: The THCPP Launch Framework (Tease / Hype / Collect / Push / Pull)
exact_steps: Five stages in order. (1) TEASE (3-4 wks before): behind-the-scenes, product obscured; every tease post should make people ask 'what is it?' (2) HYPE (2-3 wks before): lifestyle/world-building/tribe; sell the identity not specs. (3) COLLECT (ongoing): drive every post to a signup page capturing BOTH email and SMS with an incentive; target 500+ signups minimum (2,000+ = strong) before committing to bulk/full launch. (4) PUSH (launch day + 48 hrs): email + SMS simultaneously at launch time, subject line direct ('It is live'), SMS one line + link, social staggered through first 6 hrs, limited stock/countdown visible. (5) PULL (day 3 to week 4): retarget non-buyers with the organic content that performed best, plus lookalikes of list + buyers. RULE: do NOT run paid ads during tease or hype; paid only AFTER organic proves which content works.
inputs_needed: Offer/product ready, content for tease+hype, signup landing page, email+SMS platform
output_artifact: A dated 5-stage launch plan with signup target and content schedule
when_to_use: Planning any meaningful launch or drop, digital/physical/service
when_not: For a routine restock or an ongoing evergreen offer with no launch moment
example_command: os_technique_cards solve "plan the launch sequence for this offer"

problem: what to do after a winning offer / should I discount / how to grow revenue from a winner
symptom: Inventing new products after a win (kills margin); rescuing weak launches with discounts; eroding brand equity
technique: Scale-Winners rule + Variation Multiplier + Never Discount + Bundle strategy
exact_steps: When an offer hits $10,000+ in organic revenue, STOP inventing; multiply the winner. VARIATION MULTIPLIER (use in sequence): (1) colorways/material variations (add 8+ colorways, design identical), (2) format variations (port proven asset: tee to hoodie/hat/tote; spreadsheet to Notion DB to Google Doc), (3) tier variations (same core at 3 price points = stripped/standard/premium; produces 20-40% higher revenue per buyer via self-selection). NEVER DISCOUNT (absolute above commodity tier): low demand means the product/story is wrong, not the price; weak launches are not rescued with discounts; Black Friday is a trap for premium brands; use tiers, bundles, member-only early access instead of the word 'discount.' BUNDLE: combine 3-5 offers at ~70% of the sum of individual prices, framed by use case ('The complete [outcome] kit') not by '% off'; increases AOV 40-150%. SNIPED lock: trade scope not price, never race to the bottom.
inputs_needed: A proven winning offer + its revenue, list of adjacent formats/variations
output_artifact: A variation/bundle/tier scaling plan with no-discount guardrail
when_to_use: After an offer is proven and producing 10k+, or when tempted to discount
when_not: Before an offer is proven; do not multiply an unvalidated offer
example_command: os_technique_cards solve "scale my winning offer without discounting"

problem: how to manufacture physical product / avoid factory scam / supplier vetting / staged payment
symptom: Risk of being scammed by overseas factories; vague instructions; paying everything upfront; bad samples
technique: The 25/25/25/25 staged payment structure + Tech Pack + Supplier Vetting + Revision Brief
exact_steps: PAY IN FOUR EQUAL INSTALLMENTS at milestones: 25% on order placed + tech pack approved (deposit), 25% when fabric is in-house at factory, 25% on production complete before shipment, 25% on pre-shipment VIDEO confirmation of finished goods matching the tech pack. Factories refusing this rely on scam-upfront models; the structure itself filters suppliers. TECH PACK (1-4 pages, every order every time): mockup front+back, size chart in inches AND cm, graphic placement specs, fabric (GSM/composition/finish), wash/care, label/tag, packaging, quantity + timeline. SUPPLIER VETTING: filter Alibaba by Trade Assurance (escrow), require live current production video (not stock photos = red flag), response under 24 hrs, at least one direct voice/video call, sample order before bulk. REVISION BRIEF (when sample is wrong): never describe fixes in text; overlay numbered circles/arrows/labels on a photo of the bad sample, include correct reference + measurements, send as one PDF and walk through live. POD path: use Printful/Printify via Shopify to validate designs at zero inventory (20-40% margin) before moving to bulk (60-75% margin).
inputs_needed: Product spec, manufacturer/POD candidate, sample to evaluate
output_artifact: Completed tech pack + supplier vetting checklist + staged payment agreement
when_to_use: When sourcing/manufacturing any physical product or evaluating a supplier
when_not: For digital products or services (no physical supply chain)
example_command: os_technique_cards solve "manufacture this physical product without getting scammed"

problem: how to price, build a pricing sheet, 3 tier packages, what tiers should I offer, anchor pricing
symptom: Pricing sheet is one flat number or random tiers; clients pick the cheapest; no package converts well
technique: The 3-Tier Anchor Model
exact_steps: Build exactly 3 tiers. Tier 1 Entry: minimum deliverables, shortest session, the price-sensitive catcher, should feel like a steal vs Tier 2. Tier 2 Value: the one you actually want them to buy, full session + edited images + 1-2 premium add-ons, priced at 60-70% of Tier 3. Tier 3 Home Run: every add-on bundled (full production, print/album, licensing, rush), priced at ~2x Tier 2. Tier 3 is NOT meant to be bought; it exists to make Tier 2 read as sensible. Most clients buy Tier 2. SNIPED lock: Tier 1 entry must not fall below the $1,500 Reset floor.
inputs_needed: Target Tier 2 price (must be >= $1,500 floor), deliverable list, available add-ons (prints/album/licensing/rush)
output_artifact: A 3-tier pricing sheet (Entry / Value / Home Run) with deliverables and round-number prices
when_to_use: Building or revising any package pricing sheet, Reset/Op Kit/Brand System pitch
when_not: One-off custom commercial quote driven by licensing (use the pricing decision tree instead)
example_command: os_technique_cards solve "how do I structure my pricing tiers"

problem: how to write a price, round numbers, drop commas, never discount, ask budget first, price the outcome
symptom: Prices have decimals/commas, get talked down, quoted hourly, every inquiry becomes a negotiation
technique: The 4 Pricing Rules + outcome framing
exact_steps: 1) Round numbers only: $2,160 not $2,159.99. Round signals intention; decimals signal discount stores. 2) Drop commas: write $2160 not $2,160; the comma anchors the price into the thousands range, removing it scans as smaller. 3) Never lower prices: if a client cannot afford the quote, REMOVE deliverables, the price holds (SNIPED lock: trade scope, never price). 4) Ask the budget first before quoting: 'What budget are you working with?' Let the client define scope. 5) Price the outcome not the input: 'This session produces the full visual infrastructure your new website needs' justifies the fee; 'I charge $X/hour' invites an hourly comparison against their own salary.
inputs_needed: The quote amount, the client's stated budget, the business-outcome the work produces
output_artifact: A correctly-formatted quote line + outcome sentence to send
when_to_use: Writing any quote, proposal price, or negotiating a budget-constrained inquiry
when_not: Never use rule 3 as a reason to refuse scope flex; flex scope down to the $1,500 floor

problem: custom quote request, should I take this client, bad fit client, client wants hourly, client wants discount
symptom: Unsure whether to take a custom job; off-niche inquiries dilute positioning; hourly/discount requests
technique: The Pricing Decision Tree (6 gates)
exact_steps: Walk in order when a custom quote is requested: 1) Is the client within your chosen niche? If no, decline politely (every out-of-niche shoot weakens positioning). 2) Are they at or above your entry tier? If no, present the sheet unchanged (they accept or self-select out) or decline. SNIPED: entry tier = $1,500 floor. 3) Is it commercial use? If yes, price a SEPARATE licensing fee on top of shoot fee. 4) Does scope fit Tier 2? If yes quote Tier 2; if no quote Tier 3 or custom priced ABOVE Tier 3. 5) Do they ask for a discount? Do not discount; remove deliverables, price-per-deliverable holds. 6) Do they ask to pay hourly? Redirect: 'My packages are priced on the deliverable, not the hour. Here is what [package] includes.'
inputs_needed: The inquiry details, your chosen niche, your entry-tier price, commercial vs personal use
output_artifact: A take/decline decision + the correct tier or custom quote to send
when_to_use: Any inbound custom-quote request, screening an inquiry for fit and price
when_not: Pearl-network referrals where scope (not price) is the agreed flex variable; handle via referral protocol

problem: how much to charge, justify a price, when can I raise prices, defend a price increase
symptom: Prices feel arbitrary; can't justify a raise; raises don't hold
technique: The Pricing Equation + raise-justification test
exact_steps: Package Value = Time + Deliverables + Equipment + Experience. Each is an adjustable lever: Time (shoot + edit + comms), Deliverables (countable outputs: edited images, prints, albums, licensing scope, format), Equipment (gear the shoot demands; signals production scale), Experience (years, portfolio, client list, press; rises over time without the other three changing). RAISE TEST: before raising prices, ask which variable changed. If none did, the raise may not hold. If one did (new gear, portfolio milestone, new client case study), the raise is defensible to the client on logical grounds. SNIPED: payment follows proof, so a new case study / portfolio milestone is the cleanest raise trigger.
inputs_needed: Current price, what changed since last price (gear/portfolio/case study/experience)
output_artifact: A defensible new price + the logical justification line
when_to_use: Deciding whether/how much to raise prices, justifying a quote above market
when_not: Mid-engagement with a client already quoted; hold the agreed price
example_command: os_technique_cards solve "can I raise my prices"

problem: track business metrics, customer lifetime value, cost per acquisition, conversion rate, money path scoring
symptom: No idea if the funnel is healthy; pricing on single-session revenue; can't tell if marketing or sales is broken
technique: The 3 Metrics That Matter (weekly) + formulas
exact_steps: Track weekly (not monthly). CLV = avg revenue per booking x avg bookings per client x avg client tenure in years. Example: $400 headshot x 1/yr x 3yr = $1,200 CLV; price acquisition against $1,200 not $400. CPA = (total marketing spend + your time at hourly equivalent) / new bookings. Gate: if CPA exceeds 15-20% of average booking price, the funnel is broken; raise prices, cut spend, or switch channels. CR = bookings / inquiries, tracked weekly. Gate: if CR drops, the problem is the SALES PROCESS not marketing; more inquiries will not fix a conversion problem; fix the process first.
inputs_needed: Weekly inquiries, bookings, revenue per booking, marketing spend, hours spent on outreach
output_artifact: A weekly metrics line (inquiries / bookings / CR / revenue / CPA) and a health verdict
when_to_use: Weekly operator review, diagnosing a slow pipeline, scoring whether a money path is worth keeping
when_not: Not a substitute for the qualitative client-fit screen; a high-CLV bad-fit client still gets declined

problem: how to grow revenue, make more money, which lever first, raise prices vs more clients
symptom: Chasing more clients (slowest lever) while leaving price increases and upsells untouched
technique: The 4 Revenue Levers in Priority Order
exact_steps: Pull in this order, top is highest leverage: 1) Raise prices. Zero additional work, immediate margin effect. Rule of thumb: a 20% raise that loses 30% of clients still nets higher revenue with lower workload. If you haven't raised in 12 months you've already priced down by inflation. 2) Increase transaction size: upsells, bundles, premium tiers; same client, same shoot day, larger invoice. 3) Increase purchase frequency: retainers, annual refreshes, quarterly sessions; same relationship invoiced multiple times/year. 4) Increase customer count: marketing, outreach, new channels. This is LAST because it is the slowest and most expensive lever and the one most pull first. SNIPED: no outreach executed by the OS; this only scores and orders the recommendation.
inputs_needed: Current pricing, current upsell/bundle offers, retainer status, time since last raise
output_artifact: A prioritized revenue-growth move list (lever 1 first)
when_to_use: Any 'how do I make more money' or revenue-planning question
when_not: When at hard capacity and price is already maxed for the market (then go to scaling paths)

problem: cold dm, how to land a brand, product photography outreach, spec work, gifted content to retainer
symptom: Pitching brands on faith and getting ignored; no proof in hand when reaching out
technique: The Spec Work Method (product/e-commerce)
exact_steps: 1) Pick a target brand. problem: which niche, how to specialize, pick a lane, niche selection, test before committing

problem: how to test creative before spending / when to run ads / paid not converting / validate offer

problem: money path scoring / which content is a winner / how to score a post / when to amplify

technique: View Velocity Scoring (baseline-multiple gate)
exact_steps: Baseline = median view velocity of your last 20 posts on that platform. Secondary gates: Save+Share rate (saves+shares/views): below 2% = viewed not valued, 2-5% = valued, 5%+ = compounding asset. Follower-to-view ratio: below 0.3 = algorithm not pushing to non-followers (creative failing Interest Media test), 1-5 = strong, 5+ = breakout. Track velocity at 1h, 6h, 24h, 7d.

problem: copy hook / cold dm hook / first line / post not getting views / write a hook
symptom: Content body is strong but nobody watches past the first second; underperforming posts blamed on the body when the hook failed.
technique: Hook Factory (5 hook categories + 3-5 variation test)
exact_steps: Treat hooks as a separate production track. First 1-3 sec of video / first 1-2 words of post decide everything. 5 working categories: (1) CONTRARIAN: 'Most photographers are wrong about [topic].' (2) SPECIFIC RESULT: 'How I shot [image] in [short time].' / 'The setup that got this into [outlet].' (3) THE QUESTION VIEWER ASKS: 'Why are your portraits always flat?' / 'Why is your pricing not converting?' (4) BEFORE-AND-AFTER: 'This is the worst frame from the session. Watch what happened next.' (5) VISUAL SURPRISE: striking first frame with no context. Rule: every core piece gets 3-5 hook variations (same body, different first 3 sec), test all organically, winning hook becomes the paid asset. Delta between best and worst hook is routinely 5x, sometimes 20x. If a piece underperforms, change the HOOK before the content.

output_artifact: 3-5 tested hook variants + winning hook tagged for amplification

when_not: Faceless-safe note: pick hooks that do not require identity/face exposure if the lane requires it; favor visual-surprise and specific-result over on-camera contrarian if anonymity matters

problem: high views no sales / content not converting / missing middle of funnel / call to action
symptom: Lots of reach but no revenue; only portfolio (top) and pricing page (bottom) exist, nothing nurtures the interested in between.
technique: The Content Funnel (every piece has a next step; build the middle)
exact_steps: Three layers: TOP = attract new people, hook-heavy, broad, shareable (discovery). MIDDLE = nurture the interested, longer videos, case studies, content connecting your service to their specific need (the part most creators skip; where trust is built). BOTTOM = conversion, direct offers, consultations, limited-time. RULE: every piece of content needs ONE clear next step (newsletter signup, free guide, waitlist, consultation link). Without a next step even high-view content produces zero business outcome. Diagnosis: if you have top + bottom but no middle, you are asking strangers to go from 'never heard of you' to 'buy' in one step. Email list is the only owned channel; every post funnels to it.

technique: 80/20 Live Session structure (soft-pitch cadence)

Pin ONE product per session (not three; viewer holds one CTA). Mention the pinned product every 10-15 minutes, ONE sentence per mention, e.g. 'If you want the full version of this editing approach, the preset pack is pinned.' Do not oversell. A 60-min session with ~12 min of soft pitching converts better than an all-pitch session. End with a clear recap: what we covered, what was on offer, what happens next. The viewer who stays for education buys because the product is present, not because the pitch was hard. Starting cold: commit to 30 days of daily 30-min sessions, same time; week 3 sees lift, week 6 compounds.

problem: bad fit client / wrong audience / should I chase reach / high-ticket vs mass-market
symptom: Chasing mass reach for an offer that actually needs a small, specific, high-value audience (or vice versa); volume eating the core craft.
technique: Volume-vs-Depth fit test (good-fit vs bad-fit routing)
exact_steps: Run the depth model (not the volume model) when ANY of these hold: (a) solo operator with a demanding main craft where content would degrade shoot quality, (b) highly specialized niche with a small audience (e.g. ~1,000 enterprise commercial clients: one weekly LinkedIn post can beat 15 daily TikToks), (c) product requires depth not breadth (e.g. $10,000 retreats need 50-200 right-fit people, not mass reach). Depth model = 90% effort on ONE platform, 4-7 IG posts/wk done well OR one 10-20 min YouTube/wk OR one 800-2,000 word newsletter/wk, plus a direct email relationship. Decision gate: 'Has the operator tried volume and burned out, AND does the business depend on a smaller higher-value audience?' Yes = depth; No = run volume first (volume produces the data; depth without data is guessing). Community over virality: a six-figure business runs on 50-200 deeply engaged clients; track comment depth, repeat buyers, referral rate, not follower count.

output_artifact: Volume-vs-depth routing decision + good-fit audience size target

(5) Stress-test polarization: paste your offer into an LLM with 'make this more polarizing so it speaks the language of my ideal customer.' problem: how to price / discovery call / how to size a deal / quantify value / why won't they buy
symptom: Jumping to a pitch before diagnosing; deal value feels arbitrary; prospect doesn't see why to change.
technique: Gap Selling: Current State / Future State / The Gap
exact_steps: On the call, diagnose before prescribing. (1) Current State: uncover their facts, problems, and the impact of those problems via discovery, not assumptions - 'Walk me through how you're handling X right now.' (2) Impact: 'What happens when a prospect sees those outdated photos? How does that affect your close rate?' (3) Future State: paint it specifically - 'Your entire team page rebuilt in one morning' not 'better photos.' (4) The Gap = distance between the two; the bigger the gap, the more valuable the solution (a headache gap is worth $50, a brain-tumor gap is worth $1M). Help them see the gap is bigger than they thought. Ask 'why' repeatedly to reach yes. Present the solution ONLY after the gap is clear, then close: 'I can have a proposal to you by Friday. Does that work?' Core truth: no problem, no sale.

problem: money path scoring / when to scale / campaign not working / how many replies is good
symptom: Scaling a dead campaign or killing a live one because there's no decision rule on the numbers.
technique: Reply-rate decision rule (measure-week scoring)
exact_steps: Run a campaign at 8-10 emails per healthy inbox per day across ~4 inboxes; full 3-email cycle takes ~2 weeks. Then score by replies on a 75-100 lead campaign: 3+ replies = the angle works, SCALE the list (add 50-100 new leads/week to winners). 1-2 replies = test new COPY on the same list. 0 replies = the copy OR targeting is wrong, diagnose before sending more. Volume creates data, data creates clarity - you can't optimize on 50 sends, you need hundreds for statistical validity. Kill campaigns that don't produce replies; pour volume into ones that do; expand to new niches on the same proven infrastructure.

problem: emails going to spam / domain setup / deliverability / why nothing converts / inbox warming
symptom: Cold emails land in spam, domains burn, bounce rate climbs, campaign converts nothing.
technique: Sending infrastructure + deliverability hygiene
exact_steps: Never send cold email from your primary domain (one complaint tanks business email). Register 5-20+ lookalike domains (.co/.io/.info/.agency variants). 2-3 inboxes per domain, mix Outlook/Google ~70/30. Configure SPF, DKIM, DMARC on EVERY domain or enterprise servers reject on sight. Warm every inbox 14-21 days before any cold send, and keep warmup running continuously even on active inboxes. Cap 30 emails per inbox per day (campaign send 8-10/inbox/day). Verify every address before sending; randomize send times; rotate copy via spintax/variables so no two emails are identical. Monitor bounce rates weekly - if a domain exceeds 3%, pause it immediately and diagnose. Build infrastructure FIRST (Week 1); send nothing until warming completes.
inputs_needed: Domain registrar access, email provider accounts, a warming tool (Instantly built-in), verification tool
output_artifact: Warmed, DNS-configured sending stack with monitored bounce rates

when_not: One-off warm/referral emails sent from a normal inbox don't need the cold stack

problem: copy feels scattered / my sales page isn't converting / how to write an offer / writing toss-salad copy
symptom: Copy stacks multiple arguments hoping one sticks; reader confused; page tries to say everything and converts no one.
technique: The Rule of One
exact_steps: Lock four 'ones' before writing a single word: 1) One Reader (one specific business owner with one problem at one moment, NOT 'business owners'). 2) One Big Idea (a single concept that is easy to understand, easy to believe, and interesting or unique). 3) One Promise (one specific outcome, stated once, clearly, early). 4) One CTA (one action, not 'visit our site or call or email'). Then audit every sentence: if a bullet, story, proof point, or objection handler does not reinforce one of the four ones, cut it. Source datum: 91 of the top 100 sales offers in Agora Publishing history followed this rule.

problem: cold prospect not responding / copy talks past the reader / what to lead with / which message for which lead
symptom: Same pitch sent to strangers and to warm prospects; headline and lead miss because reader's awareness stage is wrong.
technique: The Awareness Ladder (5 stages)
exact_steps: Place the prospect on one of 5 stages and match headline/lead/proof/CTA to it. UNAWARE (doesn't know they have a problem): lead with a story, pattern interrupt, or provocative question; never mention the product. PROBLEM AWARE (knows pain, no solutions): agitate the pain so accurately they think you read their mind, then introduce the category of solution. SOLUTION AWARE (knows solutions exist, hasn't picked, doesn't know you): lead with your unique mechanism (what makes your approach different). PRODUCT AWARE (knows you, not convinced): stack proof (testimonials, case studies, guarantees, demos), overcome specific objections, make the decision feel safe. MOST AWARE (knows + wants it): lead with the offer (bonus, deadline, scarcity), remove last friction. Move them exactly one level closer per piece.
inputs_needed: Who the reader is and what they currently know about the problem/SNIPED.
output_artifact: Stage-tagged copy plan: chosen lead type, proof type, and CTA for that stage.
when_to_use: Before drafting any outreach, ad, landing page, or email; when a campaign underperforms and you suspect message mismatch.
when_not: When audience is mixed-stage on one surface; segment first instead.

problem: how to write a short ad / cold DM / email that sells / short copy framework

technique: PAS (Problem · Agitate · Solve)
exact_steps: Workhorse for short copy (emails, ads, social, VIB DM). PROBLEM: name the pain specifically. Example pattern: 'Your team page photos were taken at different times with different setups' beats 'your photos could be better.' AGITATE: twist the knife; show what happens if unfixed; make cost of inaction vivid. Example: 'Every prospect who visits your website sees that inconsistency and subconsciously registers: this company doesn't pay attention to details.' SOLVE: present the solution as the obvious answer, kept brief; the agitation did the selling, the solution only needs to be credible and accessible. Keep faceless-safe: no identity exposure, do not execute the send.

Clear beats clever. Run scroll-stop check before publishing.

problem: how to structure a landing page / sales page layout / Carrd page order / what goes above the fold
symptom: Landing page has no deliberate order; proof dumped in one block at the bottom; CTA buried.
technique: Landing Page Architecture (above + below the fold)
exact_steps: ABOVE THE FOLD (≈5 seconds, heaviest lifting): Headline (specific promise/transformation, clear not clever) → Sub-headline (elaborates, adds specificity or the 'how') → Hero image/video (shows the RESULT not the process) → Primary CTA (visible without scrolling, says exactly what to do) → One line of social proof ('500+ sessions delivered' or one powerful testimonial quote). BELOW THE FOLD (selling section, in this exact order): 1) Agitate the problem → 2) Introduce the solution / unique mechanism → 3) Stack proof (multiple forms throughout, NOT one block) → 4) Handle objections (price, time, trust, 'I can do this myself') → 5) Restate the offer (bundle everything they get, make value obvious) → 6) Risk reversal (guarantee / 'if it doesn't work' promise) → 7) Final CTA (repeat the action). Use ONE CTA action repeated; remove every other exit.
inputs_needed: Promise, unique mechanism, proof assets, objection list, full offer bundle, risk-reversal terms.
output_artifact: A sectioned landing-page wireframe with copy slots in canonical order.
when_to_use: Building or auditing the Reset/Op Kit sales page or Carrd; any conversion page.
when_not: Short-form (use PAS); brand-story-only pages with no offer.
example_command: os_technique_cards solve "how should I structure my Reset sales page"

problem: prospect goes quiet / how to handle objections / they say I can do this myself / proof rules
symptom: Prospect hits an unspoken objection and exits; copy makes claims about itself instead of letting others vouch.
technique: Objections-as-buying-signals + Social Proof Stacking
exact_steps: Treat objections as engagement signals: if they think 'but what about X' they care enough to buy. Anticipate every reason to say no and answer it IN the copy before they ask. Four standing objections to pre-empt: price, time, trust, and 'I can do this myself.' For proof: what others say about you is 10x more persuasive than your own claims. Stack testimonials, case studies, before/afters, specific numbers, logos, third-party validation THROUGHOUT the page (not one bottom block). Pair with specificity: '13.7 pounds in 6 weeks' / '500+ sessions delivered' beats rounded generic claims.

output_artifact: An objection-to-rebuttal map plus a distributed proof-placement plan.

when_not: Unaware/Problem-Aware leads where proof comes too early; introduce category first.

problem: cold email / subject line / how long should an email be / what to write in a cold DM
symptom: Cold emails too long, hype-y subject lines, three CTAs, never opened.
technique: Email Copy Rules (subject + body + length caps)
exact_steps: SUBJECT LINE = the headline of the email; if not opened, email doesn't exist. Keep 2-6 words. Lowercase performs better for cold/personal-feel. Curiosity ('quick thought on your profile', 'one thing I noticed') or specificity ('your team page', 're: [Company Name] photos'). Personal-feel: no emojis, no ALL CAPS, no exclamation marks. A/B test two subject lines per campaign; let data pick. BODY structure (cold/nurture/sales identical): Hook (first line, relevance in 5 seconds) → Value/insight (one useful thing they didn't know) → CTA (one action: 'Worth a conversation?' / 'Want me to send examples?'). LENGTH CAPS: under 100 words for cold, under 200 for nurture. Honor SNIPED: draft only, do not send; faceless-safe.
inputs_needed: Prospect, one relevant insight, the single ask.

problem: how to upsell / post-purchase emails / sell the next tier / Reset to Op Kit
symptom: Entry buyers never move to the next tier; no post-purchase sequence; upsell feels hype-y.
technique: The Upsell Sequence (3-email post-purchase)
exact_steps: After someone buys the entry product, run 3 emails to sell the next tier. EMAIL 1 (immediate): deliver what they bought + plant the seed. Template: 'This is Protocol 01. Pay attention to what happens when you correct the hands. That's Protocol 02.' EMAIL 2 (Day 3): expand on the result. 'If Protocol 01 changed how you approach X, the remaining 9 protocols cover everything else.' EMAIL 3 (Day 7): direct ask with personal touch. 'Did you use it yet? If it worked, the full system is here. If not, no worries.' Rule: short, direct, no hype; the product sells itself only if the free/entry asset actually delivers. SNIPED mapping: Reset deliverable as entry, Op Kit as next tier; payment follows proof; trade scope not price.

when_not: Before the entry asset has delivered real value; cold prospects with no purchase.

problem: how to write a story that sells / case study narrative / cultural-doc to offer bridge
symptom: Story is a self-indulgent anecdote; reader can't see themselves; never transitions to the offer.
technique: Storytelling-in-Copy (5-beat structure)
exact_steps: Stories bypass sales resistance, but must follow this structure: 1) Start with the struggle (establish the character: you/client/customer in a recognizable, painful situation). 2) Introduce the turning point (the moment something changed: a discovery, decision, realization). 3) Show the transformation (before vs after: specific, measurable, emotional). 4) Connect to the reader ('You might be in the same place I was' — bridge from story to their situation). 5) Transition to the offer ('That's why I built this'). Hard rule: the story is about the READER recognizing themselves, not about you. If they can't see themselves in it, it's just an anecdote, cut it. Use transformation over benefit (who they become beats what the product does).
inputs_needed: A real before/after with a turning point; the offer the story should lead into.
output_artifact: A 5-beat narrative draft ending in a clean offer transition.

exact_steps: ONE CTA per piece: every page, email, or ad has exactly one action; multiple CTAs create decision paralysis. Make the action obvious, repeat the SAME action, and remove every other exit (no 'or call or email'). Apply to SNIPED proof: 'booked 12 sessions in 48 hours' / '500+ sessions delivered' over 'lots of happy clients.' Run as a final pre-ship pass: count the CTAs (must be 1) and replace every vague claim with a specific number/timeframe.

Each rung sells to satisfied buyers of the prior rung, never cold. SNIPED LOCK: any service/DFY offer floor holds at $1,500 minimum; trade scope, never price below floor.

(e.g. 5); (3) 'What's your close rate on inbound?' (e.g. 50%). Multiply: missed leads x close rate x avg value = revenue left on the table per week/month (source example: ~$753/wk, framed as 200-320% ROI vs the fee). MedSpa variant: 5 missed calls/wk x $400 ticket = $8,000/mo lost; a $2,000 setup becomes an instant yes. Then state the offer math: 'I recover X of that for [fee].' problem: how to price a proposal / how many options / one price vs tiers / take it or leave it
symptom: Single-price proposal gets a yes/no; client shops around for a comparison; 50% of outcomes are a flat no
technique: Always present three options (never one)
exact_steps: Never send a one-price proposal. Put exactly 3 options on the page (4 is acceptable, 5+ triggers paradox of choice and immobilizes). Three changes the client's question from 'Is this worth $X?' (objective, brain can't answer) to 'Which of these is the best value?' (subjective, the question the brain is wired to answer). One price = 50% positive / 50% negative outcomes; three options drops the flat-refusal odds toward ~25%. You supply the comparison context yourself so the client doesn't leave (physically to get other bids, or mentally to imagine alternatives) to find it. For SNIPED: Reset $1,500 stays the FLOOR option; the other two anchor up. Trade scope across the three tiers, never drop the floor price.

output_artifact: One-page 3-option proposal (anchor / middle / floor)
when_to_use: Building any quote or proposal after a discovery/value conversation
when_not: Negotiating with a pure price-buyer (different play); before discovery has surfaced value drivers (high anchor will fall flat)

problem: how to anchor price / high anchor / which price first / make my price look reasonable
symptom: Middle and budget options feel expensive; client has price shock; no frame to make real price look affordable
technique: Lead with the high anchor; say the number before you show it
exact_steps: Anchoring = the first number stated skews every later judgment. ALWAYS state the highest price FIRST out loud. The anchor's job is NOT to sell that option, it is to make the other two look more affordable by comparison. Order to present: high anchor -> lowest -> back to middle (let the client ride the journey: price shock, then understanding, then the middle feels like a reasonable compromise). On the page left-to-right order doesn't matter; what matters is the first number out of your mouth. ALSO: say a price before you show a price, i.e. talk money verbally before retreating to write the proposal (e.g. 'we'll be exploring options from $Y down to $X'), which surfaces price objections early. Build the anchor by answering 'what would we do, and charge, if money were no object?' For SNIPED, the $1,500 Reset is the LOW/floor; the anchor is a multiple above it.
inputs_needed: The 'money no object' version of the engagement; stated or inferred client budget; the three prices
output_artifact: Verbal price-range script + ordered 3-option proposal led by the anchor
when_to_use: Opening any pricing conversation or presenting the proposal
when_not: When discovery has not surfaced value drivers (anchor gets cold reception); when client explicitly stated a hard ceiling and trust isn't built yet

problem: how to differentiate tiers / what makes options different / scope vs risk / build offer tiers
symptom: Tiers are just three sizes of the same deliverable (cheap=small bucket, mid=more, anchor=biggest); cup-size pricing leaves money on the table
technique: Tier on the three things a client can buy: inputs / outputs / outcomes
exact_steps: Lowest expression of options = three different-sized buckets of deliverables (valid but weak). Highest expression = three different WAYS to do business, mapped to the only three things you can sell: (1) INPUTS (time & materials, blocks of time, sprints) = client carries pricing risk, cheapest entry; (2) OUTPUTS (the deliverable at a fixed price) = price certainty, you eat overruns; (3) OUTCOMES / VALUE (paid for the result, no cap on revisions/time, possibly performance pay) = the expensive anchor, you carry the risk as a partner. The anchor is more expensive because you absorb risk and operate as a partner, not because it's a bigger bucket. Frame the spread by RISK: 'at the high option I make most of your risk go away; at the cheap option you take all the risk.' Money/profit is derived from risk (Drucker) so the more risk you remove, the more you charge. For SNIPED: Reset $1,500 = output/deliverable floor; anchor = outcome/partnership (visual system, ongoing). Faceless-safe, no identity exposure in any tier.
inputs_needed: Client's underlying goal/outcome from discovery; what they actually value (uncovered in the sale); SNIPED scope levers per engine
output_artifact: 3-tier offer architecture differentiated by inputs/outputs/outcomes + risk transfer
when_to_use: Designing the actual content of the three options, not just the prices
when_not: When you can't deliver the outcome confidently (only propose outcome/partnership if you have high confidence you can do it)

problem: what to name my tiers / good better best / gold silver bronze / pricing tier names
symptom: Options named good/better/best or gold/silver/bronze, imposing a grade and a self-serving judgment on the client's tradeoffs
technique: Name options by what the client buys, never by grade
exact_steps: Do NOT use good/better/best or gold/silver/bronze, they impose a judgment (the cheap option becomes 'the loser option') and assume you know all the client's tradeoffs (price, AND career/political risk you can never fully see). Name each option by the net benefit or what is being bought: e.g. Time / Deliverable / Partnership; or Quick-Start / Six-Month Campaign / Retainer; or by value type (Speed-to-Market, Access-to-Principals, Risk-Mitigation); or by do-it-yourself-ness ('You can do it' / 'We can help' / 'We can do it'). Names must be descriptive, not cute, not judgmental. Your job in closing is FACILITATOR, not convincer: explain the tradeoffs of each, then let the client choose. Be genuinely happy delivering ANY option you put forward; never include one you secretly hope they won't pick.

when_to_use: Finalizing the proposal labels and the closing conversation

problem: client asks how much / when to give a price / pricing too early / how to quote fast
symptom: Quoting a price early in the conversation; the earlier you name a price the lower it ends up; short-circuiting value discovery
technique: Price the client, not the job (delay the number until value is understood)
exact_steps: Rule: the sooner in the sale you offer a price, the lower it is likely to be. Do NOT quote until you've done patient information-gathering to understand the client's context and your value-creation potential. Treat a new client as a RELATIONSHIP with multiple potential projects, not a one-off job. In discovery, quantify the value: ask why they need this, what they're trying to accomplish, their numbers (e.g. sales down 10% on $100M = $10M; 20% margin = $2M of profit at stake). That value figure justifies the anchor and lets you price the client (their context) not the commodity job. For SNIPED: discovery surfaces which engine (Revenue/Audience/Reputation) and value drivers before any number, and the $1,500 floor only applies once scope is understood. Payment follows proof: do not let pricing mechanics block delivering value.

Optionally raise the typical objections yourself up front; if they balk you have a time-waster, if they engage you have a real deal (doctor-patient frame: real patients come on their own and want the straight truth). exact_steps: Reliable scripts: (1) 'It's too expensive' -> 'I understand budget is important. What was your budget for a solution like this?' then if they have no number -> 'If you don't have an anticipated budget for something like this, why do you think it's too expensive?' or 'How did you come up with that price?' or simply 'Compared to what?' I'll always be higher than them, there's a reason they're half the price. If the prices were identical, which would you choose?' then quantify value + consequence of missing the goal. (3) Parrot-back / calling out the vibe: replay their own confirmed statements ('you said this solves XYZ, you have authority to sign within budget, you wanted onboarding by this date, has something changed?') to force the real blocker out. CRITICAL constraint from source: tone must be calm and likeable (Tom Hanks tone), or these sour the call. SNIPED locks: hold the $1,500 floor, trade scope not price, never discount to win.

symptom: Prospect deflects with 'let me think about it', 'we're fine with what we have', 'not looking for that right now' and ghosts
technique: Stall and brush-off turnaround scripts
exact_steps: Scripts: (1) 'Let me think about it' -> 'We hear that all the time and nine times out of ten we never hear back. So when you hang up and call the next company, what's the #1 thing you'll be looking for?' (forces the real objection out). (2) 'We're fine with what we have' -> 'I understand change is difficult, but if you weren't considering a change we wouldn't be having these discussions.' (3) Cold brush-off 'we're not looking for anything like that right now' -> 'Most folks aren't, that's exactly why I'm calling you instead of you calling me' (then go to pain/value prop). (4) Use-the-objection-as-the-reason: '"I don't have time" -> that's exactly why I'm reaching out, this saves you time on XYZ.' (5) Time-to-close: 'I have a weekly forecasting meeting and currently have this closing by end of month, if you were me would you forecast it for that date? When would you promise it's complete?' (gets their real timeline). Acknowledge-Refer-Bridge-Move-on structure works universally: 'I understand this is a big investment, a lot of our customers initially felt the same, the reason they still bought is [USP]...' symptom: Want clients to land on a target tier but options aren't architected; no decoy to make the target look superior
technique: Choice architecture: extremeness aversion + the decoy (asymmetric dominance) effect
exact_steps: Two forces to exploit ethically: (1) EXTREMENESS AVERSION, given 3+ options people avoid the extremes (fear of underbuying at the low end, overpaying at the high end) and retreat to the safety of the middle (Starbucks dropped Short, added Venti, average sale moved to Grande). So position your TARGET sale as the middle and frame the anchor high enough to pull the average up. (2) THE DECOY EFFECT (Ariely): adding a clearly-inferior option makes a similar superior option more chosen (Economist: print-only $125 made print+web $125 look like a fantastic deal). Use a decoy to make your target tier obviously dominant. Constraint from source: don't withhold essential services just to fake tiers, each option must genuinely add value (ethical tiering). You should be happy to deliver whichever option is chosen. For SNIPED: architect the middle as the intended Reset+ landing, anchor above, floor at $1,500, nudge only via charm pricing and structure, never judgmental labels.
inputs_needed: Target tier you want chosen; a credible high anchor; a genuine (not crippled) low/floor option
output_artifact: Choice-architected 3-option layout with target as the dominant middle
when_to_use: Structuring the three options to nudge toward the intended landing tier
when_not: Don't create fake/crippled decoys or withhold essentials (unethical and erodes trust); don't use 5+ options
example_command: os_technique_cards solve "how do I get clients to choose the middle tier"
source_segment: 2Bobs extremeness-aversion lines 46-58; Dan Ariely TED decoy/Economist lines 896-924; Reddit r/sales lines 518-519

SNIPED lock: price floor holds at $1,500; if their budget is below floor, flex scope DOWN (fewer looks, fewer deliverables), never the price. Payment follows proof, so quote on proven capability, not aspiration.

problem: how to build an irresistible offer / make my offer convert / offer formula
symptom: Offer doesn't convert; prospect sees too much delay/effort and too little likelihood of result
technique: The Value-Equation Offer Build (Dream Outcome x Likelihood) / (Time Delay x Effort)
exact_steps: Architect the offer against the formula: Value = (Dream Outcome x Perceived Likelihood of Achievement) / (Time Delay x Effort & Sacrifice). To raise value, push the numerator up and the denominator down: (1) Define the concrete dream outcome the client wants. (2) Raise perceived likelihood with proof: testimonials, case studies, named-client results (not promises). (3) Reduce time-to-value (faster turnaround, same-week first deliverable). (4) Simplify effort/sacrifice on the client's side (you handle direction, logistics, delivery). Then write a single high-converting offer statement using the result. SNIPED lock: 'Proof over Promise', use receipts not bold claims; payment follows proof; faceless-safe; maximum-by-default, ship the strongest version, no baseline-vs-premium framing.

(5) Codify into a standing referral/affiliate arrangement, then move to the next 10 nodes. 10 nodes x 10-20 clients each = exponential scaling on linear effort. problem: how to make offer more attractive / is this offer good / score my offer / increase perceived value

technique: The Value Equation (4 drivers)
exact_steps: Score any offer on 4 variables. Value = (Dream Outcome x Perceived Likelihood of Achievement) / (Time Delay x Effort & Sacrifice). Numerator UP, denominator DOWN. Because it is division, driving either denominator toward zero sends value toward infinity. RULE: mature operators improve the BOTTOM (faster results, less work for the client), not the TOP (bigger claims). Hormozi calls top-loading 'easy and lazy.' For each SNIPED offer, write one concrete improvement per variable: (1) Dream Outcome (the founder's status/authority result), (2) Likelihood (proof, case studies, guarantee), (3) Time Delay (how fast they see proof/gallery), (4) Effort/Sacrifice (how little they do: full Direction Stack, we handle everything). Ship the version that moves the two denominators most.

problem: how to build a new offer / package my service / structure an offer from scratch

exact_steps: Run in order: (1) Identify the dream outcome (the founder's end state). (3) Convert each problem into a solution statement by flipping it into a 'how to...' line. (4) For each solution, generate every possible delivery vehicle: 1:1 / small-group / 1:many; DIY / DWY / DFY; live / recorded; text / call / Zoom. (5a) TRIM to only high-value/low-cost and high-value/high-cost items (cut low-value items regardless of cost). (5b) Stack and bundle the survivors into the offer. problem: how to price / should I raise prices / am I charging too little / justify premium price
symptom: Pricing at market rate, thin margin, low client commitment, attracting bad-fit bargain clients
technique: Premium Pricing + Virtuous Cycle of Price
exact_steps: Never copy the market: market-efficient pricing destroys margin. Charge until it stings slightly (the price that makes you slightly uncomfortable is near correct). Premium price is MORAL, not greedy, because: higher price drives client emotional investment, which drives adherence, which funds superior delivery, attracts the best clients, and repels the worst. The virtuous cycle: raise price -> raise perceived value -> raise results -> raise ability to reinvest -> raise delivery quality -> repeat. SNIPED lock: Reset floor holds at $1,500; trade scope not price; payment follows proof (structure the price, do not execute payment here). Direct proof point from the book: a photography portfolio company went from $300 to $1,500 average ticket (5x) and $1,000/wk to $38,000/wk profit (38x) after premium repositioning.

exact_steps: Pick the market BEFORE engineering the offer. Score a market on 4 criteria: massive PAIN + PURCHASING POWER + EASY to TARGET + GROWING. The three core buckets that always have these: Health, Wealth, Relationships. Then niche down until the TAM is still viable but small (the book uses under ~$10M/yr as the floor before it gets too small): niching almost always INCREASES revenue because you can charge more and target better. For SNIPED this validates scene-density over audience-growth (cluster depth in specific LA cultural circles) and the lineage doctrine (5 specific lineages, not 'everyone'). Founder + status/authority outcome = the wealth/status bucket.

problem: should I offer a guarantee / how to guarantee / reduce buyer risk / risk reversal
symptom: Prospect hesitates at the close, perceived risk too high, no risk reversal in the offer
technique: Guarantee Typology (4 types) + net-positive math
exact_steps: A stronger guarantee produces MORE net sales even if the refund rate rises (the increase in sales outweighs the increase in refunds, with worked math in the book). Pick from 4 types: (1) Unconditional (money back, no conditions), (2) Conditional (refund only if client did the work/met criteria), (3) Anti-guarantee (all sales final, framed as a feature for serious buyers), (4) Implied/performance (we get paid when you get the result). Structure every guarantee as: 'If you do not get X in Y time, we will Z.' Hormozi's personal favorite is the SERVICE guarantee (we keep working free until you get the result, no cash refund). For SNIPED high-ticket: use a CONDITIONAL service guarantee or PERFORMANCE structure, not no-guarantee positioning. Never offer naked unconditional money-back on a $1,500+ creative deliverable.
inputs_needed: Offer + the measurable result X + the timeframe Y + what you will do Z
output_artifact: Named guarantee with the 'If not X in Y, we will Z' statement attached to the offer
when_to_use: Building any offer; especially when close rate is hurt by perceived risk
when_not: Do not bolt a guarantee onto an offer with no measurable outcome to anchor X

technique: Bonus Stacking (add bonuses instead of discounting)

Build a stack where the summed bonus value is many times the offer price, so the price feels trivial. For SNIPED this is the mechanism for 'trade scope not price': when a prospect pushes on price, hold the $1,500 floor and either trim or stack scope/bonuses, never cut the number. Keep all bonuses faceless-safe and deliverable.

Over-deliver first to create demand flow, then monetize it, then add scarcity/price friction last. For SNIPED this directly shapes the VIB warm sequence and discovery-call design: warm via comment/value, then VIB, then discovery, then the proposal (the bigger ask comes after the relationship is built). A bad-fit signal is a prospect anchored on getting the lowest price rather than the outcome. CRM fields to capture for fit scoring: anchored-on-price? (yes = warning), dream-outcome clarity, willingness to do the work (adherence signal), budget at/above $1,500 floor, fit to one of the 5 lineages / LA founder cluster. Decline cleanly when off-scope (trade scope, never drop below floor). Conditional guarantees further self-select committed buyers (only those who do the work qualify).

problem: how to validate demand, talk to buyers, avoid false positives, do customer discovery, validate offer before building
symptom: Prospects say the idea sounds great but never buy; discovery calls feel positive but produce no sales; founder mistakes politeness for demand.
technique: The Mom Test 3 Rules (learning mode)
exact_steps: In any discovery/VIB conversation, follow 3 rules and KEEP YOUR IDEA OUT of it until you ask for commitment: (1) Talk about THEIR life, not your idea. (2) Ask about SPECIFICS IN THE PAST, not generics or opinions about the future. (3) Talk less, listen more. Never ask 'is my idea good?' Ask only about their life, past behaviors, and concrete facts.

problem: prospect gave a compliment, vague yes, feature request; bad data on a call; 'that sounds amazing' response
symptom: Conversation full of 'that's amazing', 'I always do X', 'I'd definitely buy that', or 'can you also add Y' and the founder records it as validation.
technique: Three Bad Data Types: Deflect / Anchor / Dig
exact_steps: COMPLIMENTS ('that sounds amazing') = zero data: deflect immediately, then ask what specifically would change if they had it, what they currently PAY for the problem, what they've already TRIED. FLUFF ('I always', 'I usually', 'I'd definitely buy') = false positive: anchor with 'When's the last time that happened? Talk me through it.' IDEAS/FEATURE REQUESTS = don't execute on them: dig into motivation with 'Why do you want that? What would it let you do? How are you coping without it?'
inputs_needed: Live transcript or notes of what the prospect just said.
output_artifact: A concrete past fact or price anchor that replaces the empty signal.
when_to_use: In real time whenever a prospect compliments, generalizes, or requests a feature.
when_not: When the prospect is already volunteering specific past facts and budgets, let them keep going.

problem: what to ask on a discovery call, sales script, discovery questions, cold dm questions, what questions reveal real demand
symptom: Founder runs out of useful questions and falls back on 'would you buy this?' or 'how much would you pay?', getting useless hypotheticals.
technique: Mom Test Question Bank (good vs bad)
exact_steps: ASK these (pass): 'Why do you bother?' (real problem) / 'What are the implications of that?' (must-solve vs nice-to-have) / 'Talk me through the last time that happened.' (specific past fact) / 'What else have you tried?' (urgency + competition) / 'How are you dealing with it now?' (price anchor + workflow) / 'Where does the money come from?' (B2B budget owner) / 'Who else should I talk to?' (end every conversation with this) / 'Is there anything else I should have asked?' NEVER ask: 'Do you think it's a good idea?', 'Would you buy X?', 'How much would you pay?', 'Would you ever...?', 'Do you ever...?', or any future-tense question. 'I would definitely buy that' = danger signal, not validation.
inputs_needed: A planned question list or a live conversation.

when_to_use: Drafting VIB DMs, discovery-call prep, or auditing an existing question list.

problem: how to score a lead, is this lead real, money path scoring, did the meeting go well, dead lead vs real signal
symptom: Pipeline full of friendly contacts who said 'keep me in the loop'; founder counts warm meetings as progress but nothing converts.
technique: Commitment & Advancement: the 3 currencies
exact_steps: A meeting only SUCCEEDS if it ends with a concrete next step paid for in one of 3 currencies: TIME (clear next meeting with a known goal, a real feedback session, a real trial), REPUTATION (intro to peers/boss/decision-maker, a public testimonial), or CASH (letter of intent, pre-order, deposit). Score: 'Keep me in the loop when you launch' = DEAD lead (failed meeting). 'When can we start the trial?' = real signal IF the trial has real cost. 'Can I buy the prototype/book the shoot?' = best outcome. No meeting 'went well' unless it advanced via one of these currencies. A pipeline of friendly non-buyers is a liability, not an asset.

output_artifact: A lead score (dead / warm-no-commit / advanced) plus the currency captured.

problem: cold dm, outreach message, how to ask for a meeting, request a conversation, VIB opener
symptom: Outreach asks 'Can I interview you?' or 'Can I get your opinion?' and gets ignored or feels like a time-waste favor.
technique: VFWPA outreach frame (Very Few Wizards Properly Ask)
exact_steps: Structure every conversation-request message in 5 parts, NEVER mentioning the idea/pitch: VISION (half-sentence on the world problem you're solving) -> FRAMING (where you are: early stage, nothing to sell) -> WEAKNESS (the specific thing you don't know and need help with) -> PEDESTAL (why THIS specific person can uniquely help) -> ASK (a direct, low-friction request for time). Do NOT use the words 'interview' or 'opinion' (they signal a time-waste). Framing establishes you have nothing to sell, which lowers their guard.

technique: Earlyvangelist 4-point fit screen

problem: who is my ICP, feedback all over the map, mixed signals, segment too broad, can't see patterns
symptom: After 10+ conversations the feedback contradicts itself and no clear offer emerges; founder feels busy but unlearned.
technique: Customer Slicing to a who-where pair
exact_steps: A fuzzy segment produces mixed feedback you can't learn from. Slice repeatedly: within this group, WHO wants it most? What is their SPECIFIC motivation? WHERE do they already go to solve this? Iterate until you have a tight who-where pair. Rule of convergence: you need 3-5 conversations with the SAME narrow segment to see a pattern; 20 conversations across a broad segment = one conversation with 20 different customer types = worthless. If feedback is still all over the map after 10+ conversations, the segment is TOO BROAD: slice again.

problem: should I build this offer, validate or build, what risk am I solving, new offer design decision
symptom: Founder spends months running discovery calls to confirm demand when the real uncertainty is whether they can actually deliver/grow it.
technique: Market Risk vs Product Risk separation
exact_steps: Before designing/validating any new offer, classify the dominant risk. MARKET RISK = Do they want it? Will they pay? Are there enough of them? Conversations CAN de-risk this. PRODUCT RISK = Can you build/deliver it? Can you grow/distribute it? Conversations CANNOT de-risk this; only building/testing does. Rule: do not waste conversations confirming demand when the real risk is execution. Pick the right tool for the risk you actually have.
inputs_needed: The proposed new offer and the founder's biggest open question about it.
output_artifact: A risk classification (market vs product) and the matching de-risking action.
when_to_use: Any new offer-design or productized-service decision in the OS.
when_not: When the offer is already validated and shipping; this is a pre-build decision tool.

problem: discovery call validated the wrong thing, false validation, asking detailed questions too early
symptom: Founder gets enthusiastic answers about a sub-feature but never confirmed the overall problem category even matters, producing data that looks like validation but is worthless.
technique: Avoid the Premature Zoom
exact_steps: Do NOT drill into a sub-problem before confirming the whole problem category matters at all. Start BROAD: 'What are your big goals right now?' Only ZOOM into a specific area if (a) they raise that area themselves, or (b) you have strong prior evidence it's a top-3 problem for them. Drilling into a pre-chosen sub-problem creates answers that feel like validation but prove nothing about whether the category matters.
inputs_needed: Your planned conversation flow / first questions.
output_artifact: A broad-to-narrow question sequence that gates zoom on confirmed importance.
when_to_use: Designing the order of discovery questions; auditing a flow that jumps straight to specifics.
when_not: When prior evidence already proves the problem is top-3 for this exact segment.

problem: discovery feels too formal, meeting overhead, scheduled interview, how to talk to buyers without a big meeting
symptom: Founder books hour-long scheduled interviews; 4 hours of calendar overhead yields 10 minutes of real learning, and the formality kills honest answers.
technique: Keep It Casual (kill the meeting anti-pattern)
exact_steps: Do not over-formalize early customer learning. The meeting anti-pattern wastes ~4 hours of calendar overhead for ~10 minutes of learning. Strip the formality: ask your 3 big questions in a hallway, at a conference, over a beer/coffee. Rule of thumb: if it feels like they're doing YOU a favor, it's too formal. Phone/Skype calls are a LAST RESORT, not the default: they damage the power dynamic, push the chat into formal interview mode, and prevent the relationship-building that generates warm intros.

output_artifact: A 3-question casual conversation plan instead of a scheduled interview.

problem: how to record discovery notes, CRM fields for discovery, capture conversation signal, what to log after a call
symptom: Insights get lost in one founder's head or in an unsortable notebook; the team can't review or sort what was learned.
technique: Conversation capture: signal symbols + index-card fields
exact_steps: DURING the conversation: two people max, one talks one takes notes. Record EXACT quotes (use quotation marks). Tag each note with a signal symbol that becomes a CRM field: lightning bolt = PAIN, goal post = GOAL, obstacle box = BLOCKER, workaround arrow = WORKAROUND, mountain = CONTEXT, dollar sign = MONEY/BUDGET, checkmark = FEATURE REQUEST, star = FOLLOW-UP. Medium: one insight per index card / sticky / CRM record (random-access sortable); avoid general notebooks and audio recordings (unsortable). AFTER: review with full team immediately, update the 3 big questions, disseminate (do not bottleneck in one head). CRM fields to create: quote, signal_type (the 8 symbols), commitment_currency (time/reputation/cash), next_step.
inputs_needed: Live conversation; a CRM table or card system.
output_artifact: Structured per-insight records tagged by signal type, exact quote, and next step.
when_to_use: During and immediately after every discovery conversation.
when_not: Not a substitute for the fit/commitment scoring (those are separate gates).

problem: how to prep for a discovery call, what to do before a sales conversation, scary questions, conversation goals
symptom: Founder walks into conversations without clear goals, asks comfortable questions, skips the scary one, and burns the call on Googleable facts.
technique: Pre-Conversation Prep (3 goals + the scary question)
exact_steps: BEFORE any conversation type: (1) With the team, write down the 3 BIG learning goals for this conversation. (2) Pre-guess what this specific person cares about. (3) Identify the ONE scary question you're tempted to skip and commit to asking it: 'You should be terrified of at least one question per conversation.' (4) Do all desk research first so conversation time is spent only on non-Googleable questions. Final check: if you weren't scared of any question you asked, if you talked more than they did, if they complimented you, or if you left without a known next step, you wasted the conversation. Then go build.

output_artifact: A 3-goal prep sheet plus the one scary question to ask.
when_to_use: Before every discovery/VIB conversation.
when_not: Not for an already-closed client; this is a pre-conversation tool.

problem: how to write a headline, hook not working, weak headline, copy gets ignored
symptom: Post/DM/caption/ad gets scrolled past; the opening line draws zero response; nobody reads past the first line.
technique: The Headline Carries 80 Cents of the Dollar
exact_steps: Headline is read by 5x more people than body copy, so it is worth 80 cents of every dollar spent. RULES: (1) Write 16+ headline drafts before picking one. (2) Every headline must promise a specific benefit OR deliver news. (3) Flag your exact prospect in the headline (if you serve founders, say 'founder'). (4) Always include the brand name in the headline. (5) Long headlines of 10-18 words carrying news/info outsell short ones; no readership penalty up to that range. (6) Never use a negative (reader misses the 'no'). (7) No blind headline that needs body copy to decode. Power words: FREE, NEW, HOW TO, NOW, ANNOUNCING, INTRODUCING, AMAZING, QUICK, EASY, LAST CHANCE.
inputs_needed: The product/offer, the target prospect label, the single core benefit or news
output_artifact: 16+ drafted headlines/first-lines with one selected that names the prospect, promises a benefit or news, and includes the brand
when_to_use: Writing any IG/LinkedIn opener, DM first line, Carrd headline, ad headline, email subject
when_not: Mid-thread replies; documents that are not selling anything; identity-revealing personal posts where faceless-safe lock applies

problem: which offer to lead with, what to say, untested promise, guessing the angle
symptom: You are guessing which benefit to lead with; offers get drafted on instinct then flop; no evidence behind the angle.
technique: The Promise Is the Soul: Test Two Promises Before Writing
exact_steps: Content (what you say) beats form (how you say it); the promise is the soul of the offer. NEVER guess the winning promise. Before writing a single headline, test at least two versions of the core promise against each other: show promise cards/statements to matched samples of your target and measure which they select, or run split offers and compare reply/repeat-order rates. Pick the promise that wins on measured preference, then write the copy around it. Gate: no campaign approved internally until two versions of the core promise have been tested against each other.

output_artifact: A winning promise statement (measured) that becomes the spine of the offer/copy
when_to_use: Defining a Reset/Op Kit/Brand System angle, choosing which benefit leads the pitch, before drafting Carrd or a proposal
when_not: When no audience sample is reachable yet; one-off bespoke replies; when speed beats optimization on a tiny test

problem: copy too short, body copy ignored, how long should copy be, weak body
symptom: Body of the post/pitch/email is thin and vague; it lists no facts; nobody is persuaded past the hook.
technique: More Facts = More Sales; Helpful Service Hooks 75% More
exact_steps: More facts sell more; never write short lazy copy. Readership drops fast through the first 50 words then holds steady through 500 words, so there is no penalty for long copy IF it stays interesting. RULES: (1) Pack specific facts, not general puffery. Specific + factual beats general + superlative. (2) Give helpful advice/service inside the copy: it hooks 75% more readers than product-only copy. (3) Include testimonials; they lift readership. (4) Write colloquially, as if answering a question at a dinner party. (5) Avoid bombast, literary flourish, superlatives. (6) Never write copy you would not want your family to read.

output_artifact: Fact-dense, service-led body copy in conversational voice with a testimonial

when_not: Headlines and CTAs (different rules); a context that demands brevity (SMS); when no real facts exist yet

problem: image not converting, beautiful photo no response, which image to post, caption strategy
symptom: Technically beautiful, award-style photos get likes but no inquiries; images draw admiration not curiosity or sales.
technique: Story Appeal Beats Aesthetic Elegance
exact_steps: Photographs sell more than drawings (more readers, more response). The driver of selling is STORY APPEAL (Harold Rudolph): inject mystery so the viewer asks 'what happens next?' Research finding: technically beautiful camera-club-award photos do NOT work in ads; story appeal outperforms aesthetic elegance. RULES: (1) One dominant subject. No abstract art, no close-up faces, no crowd scenes. (2) Color doubles memorability. (3) Captions are read 2x more than body copy: make every caption a miniature ad carrying the brand name + the promise. (4) Never overprint the headline on the illustration (cuts attention 19%). Gate: before any illustration finalizes, confirm a viewer would ask 'what happens next?' and that it is a photograph.
inputs_needed: The candidate image(s), the offer's promise, brand name for caption
output_artifact: Selected image that has story appeal + a caption written as a mini-ad with brand and promise

problem: bad fit client, should I take this client, good vs bad fit, screen prospect
symptom: Tempted to take an account you cannot win at, are not proud of, or cannot live with; a deal feels off but you want the money.
technique: The 10-Criteria Client Selection Gate (all must pass)
exact_steps: Accept a client ONLY if all pass: (1) Product you are proud to advertise, real personal commitment. (2) You believe you can do conspicuously better than the current provider. (3) Avoid products in long sales decline (usually an intrinsic weakness you cannot fix). (4) Client wants you to make a profit. (5) If the account is unprofitable, they at least give you a chance to do remarkable work. (6) You can live happily with the client personally. (7) Your work is CENTRAL to their marketing mix, not marginal. (8) No pure pre-launch products unless bundled with an established one. (9) Never take associations/committees as clients: too many masters, too little money. (10) Never accept an account contingent on hiring a specific individual. Fail any one = decline cleanly. Honor SNIPED lock: trade scope, never the $1,500 floor.
inputs_needed: Prospect product/history, decision-maker structure, your honest read on fit and upside
output_artifact: A pass/fail screening verdict on the prospect with the failing criteria named
when_to_use: A new lead or referral arrives; deciding whether to pitch; pre-qualifying before a discovery call
when_not: Existing clients in good standing; tiny one-off paid shoots that do not need full vetting

problem: how to price, pricing, what to charge, fee vs percentage, underpaid
symptom: You priced on a thin percentage and the work runs at a loss; you are afraid to charge for the expert, expensive parts (research, launch).
technique: Charge a Flat Fee, Make Sure You Profit, Don't Underspend
exact_steps: From the 15 good-client rules: (7) The buyer should pay a flat fee, not just a slim 15% commission, so the provider actually makes a profit. (5) Coddle the goose: launching/new work is expert and expensive, price it as such. (8) Don't haggle over bills; stinginess on research means flying blind, the buyer pays for that with bad results. (15) Don't underspend: a ticket three-quarters of the way to Europe gets you nowhere, half-funded work fails. APPLICATION: price a flat fee that guarantees your profit and funds the research/launch work; refuse to under-resource. Honor SNIPED locks: floor holds at $1,500, trade scope not price, never race to the bottom.

technique: TEST Is the Most Important Word in Advertising
exact_steps: Rule 11 of the good-client list: TEST EVERYTHING. Test promises, headlines, media, products. Validate with mail-order-style split runs, matched consumer samples, and package-promise tests, not guesses. Brands with no consistent personality become 'wishy-washy neuters'; promotions create kinks in the sales curve that make results unreadable, so isolate variables when you test. Career/agency corollary: every claim Ogilvy makes is grounded in named research (Gallup, Starch, Rudolph, Hopkins). APPLICATION: before scaling any offer, hook, or channel, run a small controlled test and let the number decide.

problem: cold dm, how to pitch, build trust, sales script, prospect skeptical
symptom: Pitches feel like puffery; prospects distrust the too-perfect claim; trust does not form.
technique: The Antique-Dealer Move: Disclose Your Flaws Voluntarily
exact_steps: From the new-business playbook: always disclose your flaws voluntarily, the antique dealers who point out a piece's defects win the buyer's trust. SCRIPT SHAPE: lead with what you are genuinely strong at, then name a real limitation/where you are not the fit, then state the specific benefit you can deliver. Pair with: informative, factual claims (not superlatives) are both more effective AND more ethical, academic virtue and commercial self-interest march together. Honor SNIPED locks: faceless-safe (no identity exposure), no outreach executed by the agent, payment follows proof.

technique: Reject Accounts to Signal Quality and Inflame Desire
exact_steps: Rules from the new-business playbook: Reject ~59 accounts per year; selectivity signals quality and inflames desire. NEVER get an account so big you cannot afford to lose it, because the fear destroys candor (and candor is what makes the work good). NEVER compete publicly when more than 4 other agencies are involved (low win odds, commoditizing). APPLICATION: pre-decide a decline cadence, walk from off-fit deals cleanly, and refuse cattle-call pitches with 5+ competitors. Honor SNIPED referral lock: floor holds at $1,500, scope flexes, decline cleanly when off-scope, don't be precious.

problem: inconsistent brand, ad hoc posting, no through-line, brand feels generic
symptom: Every post/offer looks ad hoc with no through-line; the brand reads as a 'wishy-washy neuter' with no personality.
technique: Every Ad Is a Long-Term Investment in the Brand Symbol
exact_steps: Each piece of output is a long-term investment in one consistent brand symbol/personality, not a one-off. RULES: (1) 95% of campaigns are built ad hoc with no long-term image thinking, that is the error to avoid. (2) Never be a copy-cat: no one ever built a brand by imitating competitors. (3) Promotions are ephemeral and create kinks in the sales curve, lean on durable image not gimmicks. (4) Repeat a good piece until it stops pulling in the MARKET, not until you personally get bored, sponsors tire of ads long before the audience does. (Refines the OS 'repetition > novelty' rule: measured market fatigue, not blanket repetition.)

problem: how to win a pitch, new business, land a big client, proposal that wins
symptom: Generic pitches lose; you have no edge walking into a new-business conversation; you can't break into blue-chip targets.
technique: Speculative Research Presentation + Solo Pitch
exact_steps: New-business playbook moves: (1) Pick blue-chip targets on day one and pursue them relentlessly over years. (2) ESCAPE OBSCURITY: trade-press relationships, max 2 calculated speeches/year designed for maximum stir, friends in adjacent professions, frequent direct mail to ~600 key targets (progress reports). (3) Win with a SPECULATIVE RESEARCH PRESENTATION: survey the prospect's actual problem before you pitch, then present findings, not a generic deck. (4) Sometimes REFUSING to prepare a free spec campaign wins the account (Ogilvy won KLM this way). (5) Make SOLO presentations: one conductor is more memorable than a whole orchestra in the room.
inputs_needed: Named target list, the prospect's observable problem, light research capacity, a single presenter
output_artifact: A research-led pitch (the prospect's problem surveyed) delivered solo, or a deliberate refusal-to-spec stance

problem: crm fields, what to track per lead, lead scoring, pipeline tracking
symptom: Your CRM has no fields that let you screen fit or score money-readiness; leads aren't qualified consistently.
technique: Ogilvy Fit + Money-Path CRM Fields
exact_steps: Add these fields per prospect record, derived directly from Ogilvy's selection + good-client rules: (1) Proud-to-serve? (Y/N). (2) Can do conspicuously better than incumbent? (Y/N). (3) Sales trend (Growing/Flat/Long-decline) - long-decline is a red flag. (4) Wants provider to profit? (Y/N). (5) Marketing centrality (Central/Marginal) - marginal is a red flag. (6) Single decision-maker vs committee (Solo/Committee) - committee = too many masters. (7) Contingent on hiring a specific person? (Y/N) - Y = decline. (8) Promise tested? (Y/N) + winning promise. (9) Test/proof status. (10) Number of competing bidders if a pitch. SCORING: any hard-fail (long-decline, marginal, committee, hiring-contingent) drops the lead; the rest raise money-path score.
inputs_needed: Existing CRM schema (Notion/Airtable), the lead's qualifying data
output_artifact: A set of CRM fields + a simple money-path score rule applied to each lead
when_to_use: Setting up or upgrading the lead/pipeline CRM; standardizing qualification across leads
